32. The Committee expresses its concern over the fact that a premier literary institution like the 
Sahitya Akademi is made ·to curtail its activities due to lack of funds. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends strongly that more resources be made available to the Sahitya Akademi and the arrear 
payments, if any, should also be released forthwith. The Akademi should bestow more attention on the 
development of regional languages, in addition to Hindi. 
II. Sangeet Natak Akademi 
33. The Sangeet Natak Akademi, which come into being in 1953, is a national institution engaged 
in promotion and preservation of performing arts, extending financial assistance to cultural institution 
for training and production, undertaking inter-state cultural exchange programmes etc. Although 
there is an increase of around Rs. 27 lakhs this year, as compared to the last year's Revised Estimates 
(both Plan and Non-Plan) this is negligible in view of the price escalation. The Committee is of the 
view that the outlay for the Akademi may be appropriately increased. 
III. Lalit Kala Akademi 
34. The Lalit Kala Akademi an apex institution in the field of art was established in 1954 for the 
promotion and development of paintings, graphics, sculpture, ceramics, etc. in the country. The major 
activities of the Akademi are to organise exhibitions (in and outside the country), artists' camps, 
bringing out art publications, and implementing cultural exchange programmes. 
35. The allocation for the Akademi this year has come down from Rs. 2.85 crores (Revised 
estimates) of the year 1993-94 to Rs. 2.40 crores. The Committee urges upon the Govt. to increase the 
allocation appropriately. 

National School of Drama 
36. The National School of Drama, established in 1959, is a premier institution devoted to 
imparting training in the field of theatre and to propagate dramatics in the country. Increase in this 
year's budgetary provisions for the institution from Rs. 266.65 lakhs to Rs. 285.00 lakhs is welcome. 
The National School of Drama proposes to set up regional centres, which is a welcome step, and the 
Committee desires that these regional centres should enjoy due autonomy in their functioning and not 
made mere branches of the National School of Drama, New Delhi. 
Promotion of Art & Culture 
37. A number of organisations and institutions are active in promoting and disseminating 
different types of art and cultural activities in various regions and zones of the country. A brief sketch 
of their activities, objectives vis-a-vis provisions thereof is given below:-
/. Centre for Cultural Resources & Training 
38. The Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, set up in 1979 with its headquarter in New 
Delhi, is doing a commendable job in the propagation of culture, especially among college and school 
students. One of the major activities of the Centre is to train inservice school teachers in the area of 
linkage between education and culture and to provide a cultural component in the curricula. The 
Centre also prepares audio-visuals and printed materials to be used in schools for cultural education. 
The centre also took over the scheme 'Cultural Talent Search Scholarship' from the Deptt. of Culture 
in 1982 under which 300 children in the age group of 10-14 years are awarded scholarships each year 
in various fields. 
39. The Centre has been entrusted with the task of interlinking culture with education, mass 
media and the scheme of the Deptt., bearing an identical nomenclature, has since been merged with 
the centre's scheme. 
40. The Committee is of the view that it is not practically feasible to cover whole country by the 
one and only Centre in New Delhi and hence feels the need to decentralise the activities of the Centre 
by opening sub-centres in various zones and regions. 
41. The provisions made for the Centre are not in consonance with the multifarious activities of the 
Centre. A comparative analysis of the allocation suggests that there has been a meagre increase of 
Rs. 20 lakhs in Plan and 0.65 lakhs in Non-Plan expenditure, as against the revised estimates of the last 
year. Since this is the only institution which is taking culture down to the general masses, students and 
teachers, the Committee recommends that more .resources should be allocated to the Centre, 
particularly keeping in view the Committee's recommendation for opening sub-Centres at various 
places. 
Zonal Cultural Centres 
42. At present, there are seven Zonal Cultural Centres which cover the entire country. The main 
functions of the Zonal Cultural Centres are to provide facilities for the creative development in the 
entire spectrum of culture, particularly in that of folk and tribal art. These centres are also 
implementing National Cultural Exchange Programmes, Republic Day folk dance festival and setting 
up Shilpgrams etc. For the year 1994-95 a sum of Rs. 200 lakhs has been earmarked for zonal cultural 
centres. During the year 1992-93 there was an under-utilisation of the approved outlay to the tune of 
about Rs. 175 lakhs, mainly because of the delay in allotment of land by Sta~ Government for setting 
up of Shilpgrams. The Committee, however, feels that such delays should be avoided so that funds are 
utilised in time. The Committee recommends that speedy progress be made in setting up Shilpgrams at 
the remaining six zonal cultural centres, particularly the one being set up at Thanjavur. The 
Committee also feels that centrewise allocation should also be reflected in the documents of the 
Department. 
43. Documentation and propagation of folk art constitute one of the main functions of Zonal 
Cultural Centres and as stated by the Secretary, Department of Culture, it is also one of the major 
thrust areas during this year. But the work being done in this regard cannot be said to be satisfactory. 
There is no indication as to how much money each Zonal Cultur al Centre spends on the propagation of 
the Jjving folk art forms at the grassroot level in villages where they are actually performed. Therefore, 

~he Committee is of the view that due emphasis of the Zonal .Cultural Centres should be on folk arts 
and necessary financial assistance should also be provided for the same. 
44. The Committee is constrained to note that the hopes generated at the time of establishment of 
Zonal Cultural Centres have not been fulfilled and realised. Because these centres are not pursuing the 
programmes and schemes fop which they were set up, therefore, the Committee recommends that the 
time has come for a high-powered Review Committee to be constituted to look into the working of the 
Zonal Cultural Centres. 
Dissemination of Tribal Folk Art & Culture 
45. Under this scheme, financial support is given to voluntary cultural organisations, institutions 
and individuals-both tribal and non-tribal for undertaking small duration projects of around one year 
for preservation and development of tribal folk art and culture, conduct of tribal cultural activities, 
including their festivals and festivities. This year, there has been an increase of Rs. 10 lakhs for this 
scheme. But the Committee is not happy with the working of the voluntary organisations/institutions 
in this field because it is found that the assistance does not percolate down to the folk artistes, 
although the Secretary, Department of Culture, has submitted before the Committee that Gqvern­
ment is taking necessary steps to ensure that the artistes get the desired benefit. The Committee 
recommends the pro_gressive establishment of a network of organisations to ensure that folk artistes in 
villages are enabled to derive full advantage of the scheme meant for them. Assistance should also be 
given for opening performance centres or auditoria at the village and block level so that artistes could 
perform and interact with each other to improve their particular art forms. 
Multipurpo se cultural complexes at States & National Cultural Complex in Delhi 
46. Under this scheme, financial assistance is proposed to be extended to autonomous bodies for 
settmg up art complexes in the States to improve the quality of life among youth and students and to 
sensitize them to what is aesthetically and morally good in our society and also to expose them to the 
finest forms of creative expressions. 
47. The Committee is not happy with the progress made in the scheme and expresses its serious 
concern over the fact that almost two financial years have elapsed and the projects have not been 
finalised yet. The Committee is also not happy with the idea of creating more and more cultural 
infrastructure in big cities and towns at the cost of rural areas. However, the Committee is satisfied to 
note that multi-purpose complexes, are being set up in smaller towns, rural and backward areas and 
recommends that other schemes being formulated by the Deptt. should also be located in sucn art!aS. 
The Committee also recommends that the National Cultural Complex (Parisar), proposed to be set up 
in Delhi, be established in the trans-Yamuna or outer Delhi areas. 
48. The Committee is also of the view that instead of concentrating only on huge cultural 
complexes, Govt. should set up smaller units where the deprived, under privileged and unprivileged 
may have access to all forms of culture as well as to practice and promote their arts. The Committee 
also holds that the Department may construct multi-purpose stadia in smaller towns and cities which 
could be utilised for sports during the day and for cultural purposes in the evening and night. 
Asia'tic Society, Calcutta 
49. The Asiatic Society, Calcutta, is an institution of national importance involved mainly in 
oriental studies and research, research in humanities and science, publication of periodicals, books 
and other literature. At present, there are around 12 senior fellows and 30 junior research scholars 
attached to the Society. 
50. The Committee is surprised to note that a drastic cut has been resorted to in this year's budget 
allocation for the society. The plan provision has been reduced from Rs. 341.00 lakhs (Revised 
Estimates) during the year 1993-94 to Rs. 200.00 lakhs for the year 1994-95. The provision is 
understood to have been reduced in view of the opening of the Asiatic Society, Bombay. The Committee 
desires that the activities of the Asiatic Society, Calcutta should not suffer pending opening of Asiatic 
Society, Bombay. 

51. No financial assistance has been provided to the Asiatic Society, Bombay, during the Eighth 
Five Year plan. The reason behind this is stated to be that the Planning Commission has earmarked a 
provision of Rs. 200.00 lakhs to be given to the Society as corpus fund. But this fund also has not 
reached the Society so far as it is pending approval from the Ministry of Finance. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that government shotJd expedite the matter and release the amount without 
any further delay. 
Assistance to Cultural Organisations 
52. For promotion and dissemination of Cultur¢ the Department extends financial assistance to 
voluntary organisations under various schemes such as Scheme for Building grants to voluntary 
organisations, Scheme for financial Assistance to Dance, Drama and Theatre Ensembles, Financial 
Assistance for Research Support to voluntary organisations· engaged in Cultural Activities, Grants to 
Institutions I Individuals engaged in literary Activities. 
There' has been only marginal increase in allocations for these schemes and the Committee 
recommends that they should be enhanced adequately. 
Maulana Abul Kalam Azad Centre for Asian Studies 
53. This centre, proposed to be set up in the wake of the centenary celebrations of Maulana Abul 
Kalam Azad, is still not complete. The Committee is surprised to note that this ·year budget provision 
for the Centre has been reduced by Rs. 5 lakhs, for the reasons not acceptable to the Committee. The 
Committee recommends that tLere should be no further delay in the setting up of this Centre. 
Indira Gandhi National Centn: for Arts 
54. The Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts was established in 1985 as an autonomous 
Trust. The Government had contributed to its Corpus Fund Rs. 46.75 crores between 1987-88 and 
1993-94. The balance of Rs. 3.25 crores of the Committed amount has been provided in this year's 
Budget. For the building fund, the Government has so far allocated Rs. 32.35 crores and in this year 
Rs. 16.75 crores have been provided. The Committee regrets to note that even after eight years or 
establishment of the Centre, its main projects including the building are yet to be completed, though 
requisite allocations are being made by the Government. The Committee has been told that work on 
the construction of the building has started in the real sense only in March, 1994. The other activities 
of the Centre like microfilming of unpublished manuscripts and creation and updating of data base are, 
however, in progress. The Committee feels that ~teps should be taken to utilise the funds fully and 
speedily so as to achieve the desired objectives. 
Memorials and Centenaries 
55. The Department of Culture proposes to commemorate this year the 125th birth anniversary of 
Mahatma Gandhi through Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti. But the allocation earmarked for the 
purpose is most inadequate. Also, in 'this year, the country will observe the 75th Anniversary of the 
Jallianwala Bagh Massacre but no budgetary provision has been made for this purpose. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that the budget provision for celebration of the 12Sth birth anniversary of 
Mahatma Gandhi be increased and adequate funds be allocated for the observance of the 7S.th 
Anniversary of Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.

INTRODUCTION

The main objectives of the Department of Health are:-

(i)

(ii)

(iii)

(vi)

to undertake national programmes of health and to intensify measures for the prevention,
control and eradication of communicable diseases;

to promote education, research and training in various medical disciplines, to reorient the
medical colleges in the delivery of health services in rural areas;

to prevent adulteration of food as well as drugs;

to provide primary health care at the doorsteps of the people and to train the required
number of personnel for this purpose;

to take steps for better implementation of Health Care Programmes for tribal and other

to collaborate with member countries of United Nations and International Agencies like

implemented through the State Governments and Union Territory Administrations. They include national
programmes for prevention, control and eradication of diseases.

in patient care and/ or research:

Indian Council of Medical Research, New Delhi

IL _ BUDGETARY ALLOCATION

21 A Budgetary provision of Rs. 2354.25 crores has been made for the Department of Health for
2001-2002. Rs. 1432.74 crores is the Plan component and Rs. 921.51 crores have, been provided under
Non-Plan.

2.2 On a specific query as to the projected requirements of the Department under plan 2001-2002,
the Department clarified that a budgetary provision of Rs. 1450.00 crore (including a component of Rs.
17.26 crore under Capital Head) has been made for 2001-2002 against Rs. 1300.00 crores (including a
component of Rs. 22.14 crore under Capital Head) allocated in BE 2000-2001 reduced to Rs. 1159.64
crore in RE 2000-2001. Although the BE for 2001-2002 shows an increase of Rs. 150 crore as compared
to BE for 2000-2001, there is in fact a decline in the approved outlay of Rs. 1450.00 crore for 2001-2002
vis-a-vis the outlay as projected by the Department, 1.९. Rs. 1600.00 crores. It was further clarified that
the requirements originally proposed for Annual Plan 2001-2002 were keeping in view the Ninth Plan
priorities and likely expenditure. Cut of Rs. 150.00 crore in outlay may, therefore, be restored.

XL NATIONAL LEPROSY ERADICATION PROGRAMME

11.1. The objective of the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) was to achieve
elimination of leprosy by the year 2000 A.D. by reducing the case load to less than 1/10,000 population.
The Programme received further boost in 1993-94 with sanction of World Bank assistance of Rs.302
crores for a period of 6 years. Phase I of World Bank Project was completed on 30 September, 2000.

11.2. The Committee has been informed that only 20% of leprosy patients are of infectious type and
with modem Multi Drug Therapy, the patient becomes non-infectious very rapidly. Multi Drug Therapy is
being implemented through District Leprosy Societies. The Department has informed that the World
Bank funded programme which is in its fifth year has reduced the prevalence rate from 24/10000 in 1992
to 4.1/10000 in December, 2000. To give continued thrust to 5 highly endemic States of Bihar, U.P.,
M_P., Orissa and West Bengal and also maintenance of gains in other States, the proposal for 2™ Phase of
World Bank assistance for 3 years is being prepared which is targetted for achieving elimination of
leprosy by the end of year 2003 and for completing the process of integration of leprosy services with
General Health Care.

11.3. Two rounds of Modified Leprosy Elimination Campaign a major initiative under the programme
have been implemented so far. During the first MLEC held in 1998-99, 4.64 lakhs cases and during 2™
MLEC held in 1999-2000, 2.12 lakh new cases were detected. The Committee notes with appreciation
that the Modified Leprosy Elimination Campaigns have provided the pace of acceleration for
achieving elimination by detecting and treating large number of cases even in areas where Multi
Drug Therapy (MDT) services were well implemented in last 15 years. The Committee also
expresses its satisfaction with various measures being taken for medical rehabilitation of leprosy-
cured persons.

XII NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR CONTROL OF BLINDNESS

12.1 The aim of the National Programme for Control of Blindness launched in 1976 is to reduce the
blindness rate from 1.49% to 0.3% by 2000 A.D. The budget for various service components under this
Programme has been enhanced since 1994-95 after the launching of World Bank Assisted Cataract
Blindness Control Project. Besides that, Danish and WHO assistance is also being provided for
prevention of blindness. Expenditure position has been quite satisfactory. Performance of Cataract
Operations has been steadily increasing from 16 lakhs in 1992-93 to 35 lakhs in 1999-2000. It has been
informed that the States of Gujarat, Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Delhi and UTs of
Pondicherry and Chandigarh have attained the Cataract surgery rate of 400 operations per lakh population
required for clearing the backlog of cataract blindness. However, the Committee is constrained to note
that Bihar, Assam and Orissa are among the lowest performing Sta:es having cataract surgery rate
of <200/lakh. A number of Assessment/Facility Surverys have been conducted since 1997 in a large
number of districts in the country. One of the main findings of these surveys is that cataract was still the
leading cause of blindness in 55% of blind persons. In view of the above, the Committee feels that the
Department should closely monitor the implementation of all components of National Programme
for Control of Blindness in all the bad performing States, specially Bihar, Assam and Orissa.


12.2 The Committee notes that 13 districts have been selected in Phase I of the National Survey
on Blindness, results of which are likely to be available by the end of year 2001. The Committee
feels that results when received would help in better implementation of the Programme.

12.3. The Committee is of the view that concerted efforts are required to be made for enhancing
the coverage of eye care services in tribal and other under-served areas. The Committee,
therefore, feels that this exercise should be taken up at the earliest in a time bound Action Plan.

XII NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME

13.1 The Plan allocation for the Programme has been increased from Rs.145.00 crores in BE 2000-
2001 to Rs.180.00 crores in RE 2000-2001. Apart from this, a separate provision of Rs.30 crores has been
kept for the N.E States.

13.2 The Committee is perturbed to note that HIV/AIDS infection has percolated into general
population during the past few years and presently no state remains unaffected. The National AIDS
Control Programme phase II has been launched from 9" November 1999 with the two key objectives
namely to reduce the spread of HIV infection in India and strengthen India’s capacity to respond to the
HIV/AIDS on a long term basis. There has been optimum utilisation of funds allocated for NACP -
against an allocation of Rs.140.00 crores in 1999-2000 - utilisation was Rs.135.27 crores. Similarly, an
expenditure of Rs. 168.69 crores has been incurred upto 13.3.2001 out of Rs.180.00 crores provided in
2000-2001

13.3. The Committee apprehends that very high cost of treatment of HIV/AIDS infection would
be further affected with the advent of new patent regime from 2005. The Committee takes note of
the Department’s stand that the provision for a compulsory licensing for manufacturing of drugs
for public non-commercial use should be secured. The Department is also trying to impress WHO
to use international funding for purchasing patents so that major vaccines and therapeutic drugs
including AIDS come within the public domain.

13.4... At present, 563 NGOs are being funded under the Programme. The Committee observes that
NGOs are being involved as critical partners in the following important thrust areas :-

- Targetted interventions for the high risk and marginalized population;
- School AIDS Education;

- Low cost community care for people living with HIV/AIDS;

- Counselling; and

- Family Health Awareness Campaigns.

Selection of specific NGOs and the release of funds is now being done by the State AIDS Control
Societies. The Committee has been given to understand that the release of central funds directly to State
AIDS Control Societies, instead of chanelising the funds through State Governments has resulted in better
utilisation of funds.

13.5 The Committee has, however, a word of caution. At present, what is a happening is that
that NGOs are concentrated in metropolitan cities and also where State AIDS Control Societies are
functioning well. The Committee strongly feels that the Department should conduct a survey so as
to assess which are the districts where NGO activity is simply not there and take up the matter with
the State Society for attracting NGOs towards this social activity.

13.6 The Committee is of the view that inspite of there being a fool proof procedure for selection
of NGOs under NACP, ground realities in some areas are entirely different. Regular and intensive


monitoring of NGOs is very essential for checking undesirable activities. Stringent measures need
to be taken against blacklisted NGOs. The Committee feels that besides NGOs, the Department
should also explore the possibility of involving some other agency in this area.

13.7... It has come to the notice of the Committee that research being done by Indian Scientists in
this critical area is not receiving the desired support from the Central Government. AIDS kits
developed by some Bangalore Scientists although approved by WHO did not receive recognition of
the Government. The Committee has a feeling that vested interests are coming in the way of
indigenous attempts. Government should provide all possible support, if some genuine research is
there.

XIV NATIONAL TB CONTROL PROGRAMME

14.1 India accounts for nearly one third of Global TB burden and every year has more than 2 million
new cases of TB. Based on the past experience, a Revised Strategy for National TB Control Programme
was evolved by the Government with the aim to achieve a cure rate of over 85% and augmentation of
case finding activities to detect at least 70% estimated cases. This strategy was pilot-tested with SIDA
assistance in 1993-94 on a population of 2.35 million. Since then, in a phased manner till January, 2001 a
population of about 330 million has been covered. With support of DFID and DANIDA, the population
coverage under RNTCP will be increased to about 500 million by 2002. Phase II of the Programme is
under preparation for funding under World Bank for further expansion upto 700 million population.

being available to the public in many areas, the Department is exploring the possibility of
implementing the programme through private practitioners. A pilot study on distribution of drugs
through private practitioners is being conducted in East Delhi. The Committee is of the view that
the Department should take all precautions before taking such an initiative.

steps for removing the constraints being faced by NE states which can lead to proper
implementation of all the health programmes being carried out there.

12


XVII HOSPITAL WASTE MANAGEMENT

17.1 Hospital Waste is one of the biggest health hazards that is being faced by every citizen of this
country. The Committee has been informed that 21 State Governments/Union Territories have constituted
Advisory Committees for implementation of Bio-Medical Waste (Management and Handling) Rules,
1998. The extended deadline dated 30.6.2000 to initiate treatment and disposal of bio-medical wastes for
towns with a population of 30 lakhs and above and others having hospitals with 500 beds and more has
already ended. The Committee views with serious concern that the implementation status by the
States/UTs are yet to be received by the Central Pollution Control Board.

17.2. The Committee apprehends that there are very little chances of any progress being made
and conditions of hospitals/nursing homes would continue to be health hazardous. The Central
Government cannot take shelter behind the plea that health is a state subject. Need of the hour is
that Central Government should initiate some effective steps by entering into a meaningful
dialogue with State Governments.

XVII QUALITY CONTROL OF DRUGS

Quality Control of Drugs continues to be a weak area. The Committee observes that there is a
need of taking effective steps both at the Centre and State level for strengthening the Central and State
Drugs Control Organisations. It has been informed that funds are being provided by the Centre for
purchase of equipments by State Drug Testing Labs. Similarly, additional testing equipments are also
being provided to the Central Drug Labs. The Committee is of the view that the Department should
vigorously pursue the maximum utilization of allocated funds by State Governments and prevail upon the
State Govts to strengthen the State structures by providing funds to the extent possible. The Committee
finds that Delhi, Gujarat, Maharashtra, MP, Karnataka and West Bengal are having the maximum
number of vacant posts of Drug Inspectors. The Department should take up the matter with the
concerned State Governments. The Committee is of the view that the proposed establishment of
two new Central Labs at Chandigarh and Hyderabad should be taken up on a priority basis
without any further delay.

XIX NATIONAL ILLNESS ASSISTANCE FUND

The Committee notes that there have been savings in the allocation made under National 11655
Assistance Fund due to non-setting up of the funds by State Governments. and non-receipt of proposals
by State Governments. And also due to lesser release of central assistance than anticipated owing to the
fact that States earlier sanctioned grants-in-aid have not submitted utilization certificates. Grant-in-aid to
State Governments is limited to 50% of the State contribution. Although 15 States have set up Illness
Assistance Fund, lack of resources is one of the reasons for States not contributing to this head. Besides
that, lack of publicity can also be held to be responsible for non-utilisation of funds. The Committee
feels that the Department should make concerted efforts by pursuing with State Governments to
actively implement the scheme of National Illness Assistance Fund. The Committee feels that,
public at large is not aware about the scheme. Efforts should therefore be made both at State and
Central level to give wide publicity to the scheme so that this fund could be fully utilised for the
purpose for which it has been set up.

XX GENERAL
20.1 Regarding amendment of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 and approaching a larger Bench of

the Supreme Court so that service rendered by doctors of Government Hospitals/CGHS dispensaries
come within its purview, the Department has replied that such a step would require wide ranging

13


consultations with various Ministries, statutory bodies and interested groups. The Department hag also
replied that since there is no regulatory framework for ensuring standards of hospitals and nursing homes,
steps are being taken to have a framework which could then form the basis of ensuring standards of
treatment, something which is the very basis of accountability under the Consumer Protection Act. In this
direction, two draft Bills on Clinical establishment Minimum Standard and Maintenance of Clinical
Records have been drafted by the Department and State Governments are being consulted in the matter.
The Department is also working on a draft to regulate education, training and practice of para-medical
professions.

20.2 The Committee expresses its strong reservation on the evasive stand being taken by the
Department on such a vital issue Private doctors can be taken to court for any act of negligence on
their part. On the other hand, Government doctors, by being not covered under the Consumer
Protection Act, continue to enjoy a comfortable position at the cost of patients coming under their
treatment. This kind of discriminatory position leads to serious complications in some cases. The
Committee is not convinced with the argument that standards at Government Hospitals being very
low, doctors posted there cannot no be held responsible for their lapses. The Committee, therefore,
reiterates is its earlier recommendation to make necessary amendment in the relevant Section of
the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 so as to bring Govt. Doctors within its purview.

20.3 The Committee notes that at present Members of Parliament get reimbursement in respect
of treatment taken in a private recognized hospital as per the package rates prescribed by the
CGHS. The Secretary clarified that full powers of passing bills for reimbursement of medical
treatment in private medical institutions for sitting M.Ps. and have now been given to Lok Sabha
/Rajya Sabha Secretariats. The Committee finds this misleading .

BUDGETARY ALLOCATION

The Committee has observed that allocations (both plan and non-plan) made during Ninth
Plan are invariably being reduced at the RE stage and even this reduced allocation is not fully
utilised. The Committee has been informed that non-finalisation of the procurement agencies as
well as drug supply orders under the National Anti Malaria Programme and National T.B. Control
Programme has resulted in some shortfall in Plan expenditure during initial years of Ninth Plan.
Besides that, time taken in finalisation of modalities for implementation of new projects can also be
held responsible for this trend of expenditure. (Para 2.3)

The Committee is not fully convinced with the justification given by the Department that
there has been increase in percentage of plan expenditure during the Ninth Plan period. During the
Fourth Year of the Ninth Plan, i.e. 2000-2001, Plan allocation of Rs. 1300.00 crores was reduced to
Rs. 1160.00 crores and anticipated expenditure would be Rs. 1120.00 crore. Fact remains that
allocation including both plan and non-plan component continues to be reduced at the RE stage
and even this reduced allocation is not being fully utilised. Tenth Plan is to commence from 2002-
2003. The Committee is of the view that all procedural formalities for ongoing programmes and
new projects to be taken up in Tenth Plan should be completed by the end of the last year of Ninth
Plan, i.e. 2001-2002 so that there is optimum utilization of allocated funds right from the first year
of Tenth Plan. (Para 2.4)

CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME(CGHS)

The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts should be initiated in right earnest for
obtaining usual clearances so that funds are utilised to the optimum during 2001-2002.(Para 3.1)

The Committee apprehends that exercise of creation of additional new posts under CGHS
would not be complete during 2001-2002 also which is the last year of Ninth Plan. The Committee,
therefore, strongly, recommends that the Department should make serious efforts to expedite the
creation of posts, essential for expansion of CGHS network. (Para 3.2)

The Committee is, however, of the view that inspection teams should also inter-act with
patients visiting the dispensary to have an idea about the problems being faced by them. (Para 3.3)

The Committee feels that the exercise for formulating a single comprehensive formulary for
CGHS and MSO has been dragging on for a very long period. The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends that the Department should ensure that the latest committee completes the task
assigned to it within the scheduled time limit so that a single comprehensive drug formulary for
CGHS and MSO is brought out without any further delay. (Para 3.4)

SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL

The Committee expresses its serious concern on the declining trend in the utilization of Plan
allocation for Safdarjung Hospital as indicated below:-

I.          INTRODUCTION
1.1       India with just 2.4% of the world landmass constitutes 16% of the present world population.  The census of 1991
had indicated the population of India as 846.3 million.  In the decade of 1981-91, 163 million persons were added to the
population of India.  On 11 th May, 2000, the population of India has already crossed 1 billion mark.   If the present rate
of annual growth of population  of 1.74% continues, India may overtake China in 2045 to become the most populous
country in the world.
1.2      With a view to check  the growth of population, the Family Welfare Programme was taken up with the
introduction of Planning in the country.  The objective of the Family Welfare Programme for the country has been to
stabilise population at a level consistent with the needs of national development.  To achieve this goal the Department
continues to implement the three-pronged strategy of :
(i)         improvement in the health status of women and children;
(ii)        fulfillment of the unmet needs of contraception with a special focus on widening the range of choice

accepting the responsibility of funding all the existing sub-centres in exchange for the States accepting the financial

effective implementation of the scheme.

V.           REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH  PROGRAMME (RCH)
5.1.         The concept of RCH Programme is to provide need-based, client-oriented, demand-driven, high quality and
integrated RCH services to the beneficiaries. The RCH programme is a composite programme incorporating the inputs
of the Government of India as well as funding support from external donor agencies including the  World Bank and the
European Commission. 
5.2.         The Programme aims at meeting the unmet needs of Family Welfare Programme by improving health status of
women and children, especially the poor and underserved, by reducing infant, child and maternal mortality and
morbidity through:-
 
(a)
          Sustaining and strengthening the ongoing Child Survival and Safe Motherhood Programme to ensure the
essential services as per package of services;
(b)         Improving the performance of the Family Welfare System in implementing policy change;
(c)          Strengthening  the quality and effectiveness of the services under essential package of Reproductive and
Child Health Services;
(d)         Improving project implementation through the application of performance based criteria for continued
funding; and
(e)          implementing and managing project activities by following certain fixed benchmarks.
5.3.         Allocation of Rs.951.00 crores was made in BE 2000-2001 which was reduced to Rs.801.00 crores at the RE
stage. Allocation in BE 2001-2002 has been substantially enhanced to Rs.1126.95 crores. On being asked as to how the
additional allocation will be utilized, the Department informed that the additional allocation is because of release of
funds direct to SCOVA Committees formed in the States to avoid delay while routing funds through the State Finance
Departments. The increase is proposed to be utilized in the following components.

category C districts.
(ii)                Dais Training
(iii)               Out-reach Services – Presently being implemented in 50 districts, proposed to be extended to
another 100 districts covering thereby 150 districts in all.
(iv)              Hepatitis-B Project – A new Pilot Project on Hepatitis B at a cost of Rs.9.27 crores proposed to
be taken up during 2001-2002.
(v)                Financial Envelope – Currently, provided to 4 States only, proposed to extend it to 2 more
States during the next year.

However, allocation in BE 2001-2002 has been increased mainly due to more demand of free supply of Nirodh from the
State Governments. The increase in allocation in 2001-2002 is also due to the fact that cost of raw material has been
added in the proposed BE as UNFPA  has discontinued the supply of  raw material as commodity assistance for
manufacturing  of Oral Contraceptive pills.
11.2.   The Committee has been informed that according to the studies conducted by the International Institute of
Population Studies, Mumbai in Haryana, Maharashtra and UP revealed that around sixty percent of condoms under free
distribution system was unused and wasted.  Hence, in order to minimize wastage and promote distribution of
comdoms, a scheme of service charge of ten paise per condom, to be retained by the health worker, was introduced
during 1997-98.  However, subsequent survey revealed that this new incentive did not reach most of the doctors and
health workers in PHC/ Sub Centres.
11.3.    The Committee feels that the scheme of service charge of ten paise per condom to be retained by the health
worker is  good except for the fact that ten paise per condom is too meagre an amount to attract the enthusiasm of the
health workers.  The Committee is also disturbed to know that this new scheme did not reach most of the doctors and
health workers in the sub centres.  This means that the funds  earmarked for the purpose are being squandered by the
middlemen instead of reaching the health workers.  The Committee views this as a serious lapse in monitoring the
utilization of funds by the Department and recommends that  corrective measures may be taken in this regard.
XII.         STERILISATION BEDS
12.1.       Under this Scheme, maintenance grant @ Rs.4500/- per annum is paid to each institution subject to a condition
that a minimum of 75/60 tubectomics per bed per annum are achieved by the Government/Voluntary Agencies
respectively. At present 3115 beds are functioning which is 58 below the last year’s figure of 3173.
12.2.       The Committee notes that the allocation under ‘Sterilisation Beds’ for 2000-2001 was Rs.1.70 crores.   The
Department has informed that a proposal to enhance the maintenance grant to Rs.6500 has not been implemented, so, far
and once they are revised the requirement shall be around Rs.2.02 crores.  The Committee  observes that since 1998-99
same level of allocation is being made under this scheme which indicates that there has been no increase in the numbers
of Sterlisation Beds during this period.   What is more disturbing that during 2001-2002, a reduced provision of Rs. 1.35
crores is proposed.
12.3.
              The Committee has been given to understand that after vigorously pursuing with the State Governments  for
augmentation of Sterlisation Beds, proposals from 16 NGOs for 54 Beds have been received from Tamil Nadu, West
Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Kerala in 2000-2001 which  have been sanctioned by the
Department.
12.4.              The Committee recommends that the Department should take necessary steps to  increase the number of
sterlization beds, particularly in the more populated states of the country.   The Committee also recommends that the
proposal of revision of maintenance grant from Rs. 4500/- per bed per annum for   Rs.6500/-  per bed annum which is
under consideration for long may be expedited.
XIII.        NATIONAL POPULATION POLICY
13.1.       The Committee notes that after many years of deliberation and consultation, the National Population Policy,
was presented to Parliament last year.  The Committee has been informed that the immediate objective of the National
Population Policy is to address the unmet needs of contraception, health infrastructure, health personnel and to provide
integrated service delivery for basic reproductive and child health care.  The medium term objective is to bring the total
fertility rates to replacement level by 2010 through vigorous implementation of intersectoral operational strategies. The
long term objective is to achieve a stable population by 2045, at a level consistent with the requirement of sustainable
economic growth, social development and environmental protection.

13.2.       The Committee has been given to understand that a number of new structures, i.e. National Commission on
Population, State/UT Commissions on Population, Coordination Cell within the Planning Commission and a
Technology Mission are proposed.  The Committee has been informed that the First meeting of the National
Commission of Population was held  on 22
nd July, 2000 under the Chairmanship of Prime Minister where the following
policy  decisions were taken:
1.                   Setting up a National Population Stabilisation Fund with seed money of Rs.100 crores to support project
contributing to population stabilization. It is expected that trade, industry, corporate sector as also individuals
will contribute to this fund.
2.                   Setting up an Empowered Action Group presided by Minister of Health & Family Welfare     for area
specific programmes with special emphasis on States that have been lagging behind  in containing population
growth.
3.
                  The National Commission on Population decided to constitute Working Groups on the following
subjects:-
                       -           Unmet needs for contraception, material and child health.
-           Unmet needs of other social sectors like health, women’s development, nutrition, water supply and
sanitation.
           -           Primary and Secondary Education in relation to population stablization.
-           Registration of births, deaths and marriages.
           -           Media for IEC and motivation.
-           Mainstreaming of Indian System of Medicines and Homoeopathy.
            -         Adolescents
            -         Mechanism for monitoring by the Commission.
            -         Involvement of civil society, including industry, labour and NGOs.
13.3.       The Committee feels that there should be a consensus at the political level as to how to implement the
population policy. The political parties have to consciously take a decision in this regard and rise above their electoral
considerations. The Committee has also noted  that where there is  higher literacy particularly amongst women, the rate
of growth of population is on the decline. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should focus
more and more on education of women in its IEC activities.
XIV        TRAINING, RESEARCH AND EVALUATION
14.1.       A provision of Rs.93.35 cores in BE 2000-2001 for ‘Training, Research and Evaluation’ was reduced to
Rs.90.25 crores at the RE stage.   BE for 2001-2002 has been increased to Rs.122.61 crores.  To a query as to in what
manner the additional fund is proposed to be utilized, the Department has replied that the additional funds are provided
mainly for staff salaries, contingencies, POL, rent for training schools/hostel buildings and training of medical and para-
medical staff and enhancing research activities.
14.2.       The Committee has been given to understand that based on 1998-99 survey, there are 142 districts in the
country where the cases of safe delivery is below 30%. Most of these districts are in U.P., Bihar, M.P., Rajasthan and
Orissa. The Department also informed that in order to facilitate safe delivery,  it has been decided to give theoretical and
practical training to one Dai in each revenue village. These Dais are to be given medical kits and training so that they
use these kits effectively. They are also to be taught as to how to identify difficult delivery cases so that such difficult
cases are referred to the ANMs or Lady Health Visitors.
14.3.       The Committee is deeply distressed to know that the percentage of safe delivery in some States is below 30%.
The Committee though appreciates the efforts made by the Department to train Dais in this regard but feels that the
gravity of the problem is too big to be tackled by a few trained Dais.   The Department would have to give a serious
thought to this situation, particularly with reference to comparatively vulnerable States where the position of safe
delivery is really grim.

I           INTRODUCTION
1.1       The Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM&H)  was set up by the Government of
India as an independent Department in March, 1995 under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.  The main
objective of the Department is to develop and promote Indian Systems of medicine, namely, Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani,
Homoeopathy, Yoga and Naturopathy in an organized and scientific manner in the country.
1.2       For the 9
th Five Year Plan, the Department identified the following six thrust areas for the development and
growth of systems.
Improvement and upgradation of standards of education in ISM&H

XV       PATENT CELL AND TRADITIONAL KNOWLEDGE DIGITAL LIBRARY (TKDL)
15.1     Patent Cell (ISM)  was created in the Department on 22.4.97 to look after the work relating to :-
To keep track of patents being filed in India or other parts of the world with respect to Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani
Drugs and Patent proprietary medicines.
To extend professional assistance to organizations and scientists in the ISMH Sector in connection with the filing of
Patents by providing information contained in ancient texts.       
15.2     The Department has informed that after observing the work  of the Cell and after visiting the World  Intellectual
Property Organisation it was realized that there is not much scope  for such a Cell.  By establishing a Traditional
Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL), the need of a legal expert will not be there.  Whenever there is any controversy  it
can be effectively countered by effective use of knowledge and advanced technology.   The Director, NISCOM was also
of the  view that after establishment of TKDL, the patent cell would become redundant because patents are valid only
within a country and patents are generally published only after they are granted and not before.   Moreover, the Patent
Cell of the Department would not be able to access any information at the time of filing  patents, and the cell   would be
useful only for filing of patents by Research Councils working under the Department.
15.3     The Department further informed that with the help of TKDL, the accessibility of information would  become
easier and nobody can claim to have innovated or discovered on 14 items mentioned in the TKDL.  Ayurveda Experts
would also be recruited for giving expertise in regard to plants and other things and this would also find place side by
side in the 14  TKDL texts  which would be completed within eight to ten months.   Unani and Siddha experts would
also be encouraged  to do a similar exercise.
15.4     The Department also informed that the research councils have already documented 4,500 items of traditional

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
1.1       With the Constitutional mandate of 1950  under Article 45 Chapter IV, Directive Principles of State Policy,
which states “the State shall endeavour to provide within a period of ten years from the commencement of this
Constitution for free and compulsory education to all children until they complete the age of 14 years”  and efforts of
83
rd Amendment focussing on making Elementary Education a Fundamental Right, provision of universal elementary
education has been strongly upheld and  made a salient feature of National Policy since independence.   This resolve has
been vigorously spelt out in the National Policy on Education (NPE) 1986 and the Programme of Action (POA) 1992.   
Social justice and equity are by themselves a strong argument for providing basic education for all.   It is an established
fact that basic education improves the level of human well-being especially with regard to population control, life
expectancy, infant mortality, nutritional status of children etc.   Studies have also shown that universal basic education
significantly contributes to economic growth.
II         ELEMENTARY EDUCATION STATUS
2.1       As compared to 1950-51, the number of Primary Schools which was 2.10 lakh with 5.38 lakh teachers has grown
up to 6.27 lakh Primary schools with 19.04 lakh teachers in 1998-99.   Similarly, there were 13,596 upper primary
schools with 86000 teachers in 1950-51 which has increased to 1.90 lakh upper primary schools with 12.78 lakh
teachers.   Similarly, in 1950-51,   19.50 million children were enrolled which increased  to 150 million in 1998-99.
2.2       As per Census 1951, the literacy rate which was 16.67%  rose to 52.2% in 1991 and 62% in 1997 as per National
Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO) 53
rd round survey.   If the rate of growth of literacy is compared with 1951 it is
seen that during 1951 to 1991  it increased at  a slow pace.   However, if the rate of growth between 1991 and 1997 is
taken into account it  will be seen that it has increased around 10% in a short span of 6years showing 1.6% rate of
growth per year.   If this is taken as the base, then it is expected that the target of 75% literacy could perhaps be
achieved by the end of 2005 as envisaged by National Literacy Mission.  According  to the NSSO Survey (53rd Round),
the female literacy rate rose from 39.3% in 1991 to 50 % in 1997 and the rural literacy rate increased from 44.7% to
56% during this period.  The Committee feels that NSSO figures are highly misleading as the samples chosen are not
really representative samples.   Both NSSO figures and other indicators may hold good so far as the Country as a whole
is concerned, but the reality in the field is totally different. Though these figures may give the impression that the gender
gap and urban rural differential has reduced considerably, the gap between Male-female Literacy, urban-rural literacy,
literacy amongst SCs/STs and other weaker sections is still a cause of concern for the Committee.   The Committee is
conscious of the fact that in certain Tribal dominated areas in the country, literacy among males is very low and
particularly among females is even less than 2% especially in the State of Orissa.  The Committee is of the considered
view that balanced growth will not be possible in case this gap is not bridged by taking special care of such weaker
groups.   Such groups will have to be brought to the mainstream by educating them and providing all possible
assistance.
III        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
3.1       The Ninth Plan allocation for Elementary Education and Literacy has been Rs. 16,999.98 crores against Rs.
4,280.00 crores in Eighth Five Year Plan.   The projected requirement of Ninth Plan was Rs. 63118.98 crores.   The
Secretary, Department of Elementary Education and Literacy stated that expenditure during four years of the Ninth Plan
was Rs. 11324.96 crores which was approximately 66.62% of the entire allocation.   Taking  this into account Rs.
5675.02 crores is available for allocation for 2001-2002.   The projected  requirement was Rs.5,227.40 crore. However,
actual allocation made is Rs.4,000 crore which shows a shortfall of Rs.1227.40 crores. The allocation for 2001-2002 for
the major schemes of the Department are as under:-

3.2       The Committee notes that the plan allocation of Rs.3728.75 crore for elementary education in 2000-2001 was
reduced to Rs.3250.00 crore at the RE stage and against this reduced allocation, expenditure reported upto 16
th
February, 2001 is only Rs.2601.89 crore. This has been there for all the four years of the Ninth Plan.  The Committee
suggests that all the Schemes should be included in the Budget only after the approval of all the concerned
Departments.   The present practice should be stopped forthwith.  It has been informed that the long process of approval
of a number of programmes like Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA), Education Guarantee Scheme and Alternative and
Innovative Education Scheme etc. has adversely affected the utilization of funds as only planning activities could be
initiated during 2000-2001. The Committee has noticed the trend of under-ulitisation during 1999-2000 also. The
Committee hopes that as substantial work in building up capacity of States to undertake the planning exercise has
already been initiated, SSA and EGS and AIE Scheme would be effectively launched during 2001-2002 leading to
optimum utilization of allocated funds.
PERFORMANCE BUDGET
3.3       The Committee is of the view that the present document of Performance Budget is anything but Performance
Budget.  It merely gives description  of the Schemes which in fact is also necessary.  The Performance Budget is
expected to give the quarterly financial and physical targets and authorities  responsible for implementing the same. 
There should be monitoring by a joint Committee of Centre and State.
IV        UNIVERSALISATION OF ELEMENTARY EDUCATION
4.1       Last year, the Committee was given to understand that the revised 83
rd Constitution Amendment Bill, 1997 to
make education for children from 6-14 years of age a Fundamental Right had been referred to a Group of Ministers for
detailed examination of financial and legal aspects. As per the latest information, the 83
rd Constitution Amendment Bill
is still under consideration of the Group of Ministers.
4.2       The Committee strongly recommends that the Constitutional obligation of making free and compulsory
education upto the age of 14 years be declared as a Fundamental Right.  The Bill should be brought before the
Parliament without any loss of time.
V         OPERATION BLACKBOARD
5.1       The Scheme of Operation Blackboard was started in the year 1987-88 to bring all existing primary schools in the
country to a minimum standard of facilities by providing them with:-
at least two reasonable large all weather rooms along with verandah and separate toilet facilities for boys and girls;
at least two teachers as far as possible one of them a woman; and
essential teaching and learning material.
The Scheme has been expanded to provide a third room/ teacher to primary schools where enrolment exceeds 100 and to
extend the same to the upper primary schools from 1993-94. The Scheme is implemented through State
Governments/UTs through 100% Central assistance for procurement of teaching learning material and appointment of
additional teacher in single teacher schools. However, construction of school buildings is the responsibility of the State
Governments.
5.2       The Committee while appreciating the lofty objective of introducing Operation Blackboard is of the view that
Government have miserably failed in achieving those objectives. In most of the schools in the country these minimum
facilities hardly exist. There are many schools which have only one teacher. The Committee cannot think of a single
teacher school because of its inherent constraints. The Committee strongly recommends that the concept of single
teacher school should be stopped without any loss of time as it is not serving any useful purpose. The Committee is of
the opinion that in every school there should at least be two teachers by the end of Ninth Plan.  There is a provision for
additional teachers for far flung areas which are normally the tribal areas and 50% of the teachers have to be lady
teachers.  These lady teachers should be asked to join in their assigned rural areas and all the State Governments may be
requested to implement the Scheme for better enrolment of girls in these areas.

and State Governments in a ratio of 75:25 during the Tenth Plan and 50:50 thereafter would be acceptable to the State
Governments.  Most of the State Governments due to their financial constraints find it difficult to shoulder this
additional liability. The Committee, therefore, feels that the schemes should be formulated in such a way that State
Governments could find it convenient to accept the liability when it comes to them. It should be understood that
effective implementation of any scheme, which has to be done by the State Governments, is not possible without the full
cooperation of the States.
5.5       As per the Performance Budget 2000-2001 of the Department, NIEPA, which  was assigned the task of assessing
quantitative and qualitative progress made in the implementation of the scheme in 1997-98  is yet to submit its report.   
The Committee regrets that the report of NIEPA is still awaited and wishes that the report should be finalized, studied
and remedial measures taken by the Department at the earliest.   
VI        NON-FORMAL EDUCATION PROGRAMME
6.1       The programme was launched in 1979-80, particularly for those children especially girls and working children
whose participation in the school system was thwarted by socio-economic conditions.  The programme was revised in
1993, with emphasis on organizational flexibility, relevance of curriculum, diversity in learning, activity to suit the
needs of learners through decentralized management.  The main focus of the programme was on the educationally
backward States of Andhra Pradesh, Arunanchal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Jammu & Kashmir, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa,
Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal.  After evaluation of the programme by the Planning Commission, and also
in the light of feedback received from various studies, the Prgramme of non-formal education has since been revised and
named Education Guarantee Scheme and Alternative and Innovative Education (EGS&AIE).  The revised scheme
envisages the following strategies:-
Setting up of schools in schoolless habitations (EGS)

6.2       The scheme has all-India coverage with priority to ten educationally backward States as stated above.  The ratio
of sharing of expenditure between Centre and State is 75:25.  The Central assistance is 100 per cent for centres run by
voluntary agencies, whose number is 816 at present.  Since a lot of preparatory work, such as micro-planning, school
mapping exercise, setting up of state level societies, etc. is to be carried out by States/UTs for operationalisation of  the
revised scheme,  it would  be fully implemented with effect from 1st April, 2001.  However, EGS component could be
operationalised during 2000-2001.
6.3       As per the sixth All-India educational survey 1993, there were 1,76,523 schoolless habitations out of 10,60,612
total habitations in the country which did not have a learning centre within one kilometre.  The Committee does not
know whether the Department has any time-bound strategy to cover these unserved habitations.  The Committee would
like to know in what manner the Department proposes to cover the habitations as the number of such habitations is quite
large. 
6.4       As per the revised EGS&AIE, the unit cost per child per annum has been revised from Rs. 375 to Rs.845 for an
EGS primary centre and from Rs.580 to Rs.1200 for an upper primary centre.  Similarly, honoraria of instructors and
supervisors have been enhanced to Rs. 1000 per month and Rs.1500 per month respectively.  The annual allocation for
teaching learning material and cost of training of instructors have also gone up.  In view of this increase, the enhanced
B.E. allocation of Rs. 400.00 crore for 2001-2002 is likely to be fully utilized, the Department has informed.
 Since the beginning of the Ninth Plan, allocation for Non-Formal Education Scheme is being drastically reduced at the
RE stage and even that reduced allocation could not be fully utilized, the Department has informed, as the scheme was
under revision during this period.  The Committee feels that the change has taken place only in the nomenclature, the
new Scheme will be continuing on the same pattern as the earlier one.  The Scheme has totally failed.  The Committee
considers this as wasteful expenditure. 
VII       DISTRICT PRIMARY EDUCATION PROGRAMME (DPEP)
7.1       The Centrally sponsored scheme of District Primary Education Programme (DPEP) was launched in 1994 as a
major initiative to revitalize the primary education system and to achieve the goal of universalisation of primary
education.  The programme adopts a holistic approach to universalize access, retention and improved learning
achievement and to reduce disparities among social groups.  The programme primarily aims at providing access to
primary education for all children, reducing primary drop-out rates to less than 10 per cent, increasing learning
achievement of primary school students by at least 25 per cent and reducing the gap among gender and social groups to
less than 5 per cent.  85 per cent of the project cost is shared by the Central Government and 15 per cent by the State
Governments.  The Central share is resourced by external funding.  The programme which was initially launched in
1994 in 42 districts of 7 States has now expanded to cover 248 districts of 18 States.  The programme is to be further
expanded in 8 districts of Orissa, 9 districts of Rajasthan and 6 districts of Gujarat.  Under the programme, 10,000 new
primary schools have been opened and 53,000 alternative schooling centres have been set up, so far.  Besides this,
15,000 new school buildings and 24000 additional class rooms have been constructed, apart from repairing of 6000
school buildings.  A provision of 25,000 units of drinking water and toilet facilities have also been provided in the
schools. The Committee recommends that drinking water facility and toilets should be made the integral component of
DPEP and these facilities must exist in every school under DPEP.
7.2       There has been  by and large full utilisation of funds allocated under this programme since 1993-94 although
instances of reduction at the RE stage are there. The allocation for DPEP in 2000-2001 was Rs.969.00 crores which was
reduced to Rs.820 crores at R.E.  stage.  Asked as to the reason for this reduction, the Department clarified that the B.E.
allocation for 2000-2001 was reduced to Rs.820 crores in spite of the proposed requirement of Rs.1056.00 crores.  The
B.E. 2001-2002 is Rs.1100.00 crores which will meet the requirement of funds for the on-going programmes as well as
meet the requirements for the proposed expansion of DPEP in additional districts of the States of Rajasthan, Orissa and
Gujarat.  The Committee expresses its unhappiness over the drastic cut at the R.E. stage in 2000-2001 and hopes that
there will not be any cut in R.E. 2001-2002.
 7.3      According to the Department, the reviews and various evaluations studies of the programme have brought out
that the programme has resulted in significant increase in enrolment, improvement in learning achievement, reduction in
repetition rates/dropouts with increased community involvement and improvement in classroom processes. However,
the Committee observes that the enrolment trend of DPEP phase I indicates that the increase in enrolment is not
uniformly  maintained in States of Assam, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.  Similarly, with regard to the number of children
enrolled in phase II districts, there is a declining trend with respect to the States of Bihar, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.  The

VIII      NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT TO PRIMARY EDUCATION (MID-DAY
MEAL PROGRAMME)
8.1       The Mid-day Meal Programme was launched on the 15th August, 1995 to give a boost to universalisation of
primary education and simultaneously emphasizing on nutrition of students in primary schools.  The scheme aims at
providing wholesome cooked/processed food through local bodies such as Panchayats and Nagar Palikas.  Under the
scheme, food grains (wheat/rice) at the rate of 3 kg. per student per month is being distributed to all children in primary
classes studying in Government, local bodies and Government-aided schools, subject to a minimum attendance of 80
per cent in month.   The idea under the scheme was to give foodgrains  initially and subsequently switch over to serving
of cooked food.  However, even after the passage of five to six years after the launching  of the scheme, most of the
States are still distributing foodgrains to the students,  due to various difficulties being faced by them, such as constraint
of resources, inadequate cooking arrangements and resentment among teachers.  Only a few States like Gujarat, Kerala,
Orissa, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh and Pondicherry serve cooked food to the eligible children.  The Department has
been persuading the States to change to hot cooked meals but so far it has not been successful.
8.2       The programme covers 9.90 crore children in about 7.14 lakh schools in the country and perhaps it is  the largest
programme in the world.  While the programme has reportedly given a boost to enrolment in the States of Assam,
Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal, it had positive impact in other States on school attendance and
retention.

other Elementary Education Schemes, voluntary agencies should not be involved in the implementation of this Scheme.
The Committee notes that in a recent meeting with State Secretaries, State Governments were impressed upon to
provide hot cooked meals to students. The Committee has been given to understand that there is a proposal to suitably 
modify the scheme which would get implemented with the onset of Tenth Plan.  The Committee would like to be

XVI     ADULT EDUCATION
16.1     With a view to bringing total literacy in the country, the National Literacy Mission was set up in 1988.   The
goal of the Mission  now stands at attaining a sustainable, threshold level of 75% functional literacy by 2005.   Total
Literacy campaigns (TLCs) is the dominant strategy of NLM for implementation of literacy programmes.   They are
area-specific, time-bound, volunteer based, cost effective and outcome-oriented and aim to impart functional literacy to
the learners.   TLCs are implemented by Zilla Saksharata Samitis (ZSS), normally headed by the District Collector.   As
on date, out of 588 districts in the country, 559 districts have been covered under literacy campaigns.
16.2     The Committee is not convinced with the impact of Total Literacy Campaigns  as ground reality seems to be
entirely different, Under the banner of these campaigns, only processions of school children are being taken out.
Experience of Public representatives is that funds released for these campaigns are being misused by District
Collectors.   The Committee is of the opinion that Panchayats and Village Education Committees should also be
involved in this exercise.   Another suggestion is that instead of making TLC Volunteer-based, high school students can
be involved in the work of adult education.   The Committee has been informed that a panel of external evaluation
agencies has been drawn up who conduct the evaluation of the districts as per the norms and guidelines laid down by the
National Literacy Mission.   The Committee would like to be apprised about the findings of these reports, which at
present, are being summarized.

            The Committee has been given to understand that the Department is contemplating to involve the voluntary
agencies in the implementation of Mid-Day Meal Scheme. The Committee has its own doubts about effectiveness of
this proposed move. The Committee feels that in the light of experience gained on involvement of voluntary agencies in
other Elementary Education Schemes, voluntary agencies should not be involved in the implementation of this Scheme.
The Committee notes that in a recent meeting with State Secretaries, State Governments were impressed upon to
provide hot cooked meals to students. The Committee has been given to understand that there is a proposal to suitably 
modify the scheme which would get implemented with the onset of Tenth Plan.  The Committee would like to be
apprised in this regard.   The Committee reiterates  its earlier recommendation that only hot cooked meals should be
served to the students under Mid-Day Meal Scheme. (Para 8.5)
SARVA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN (SSA)
The Committee has its own reservations on the financial norms laid down under Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA). In view
of financial constraints of State Governments, it is doubtful whether the financial norms indicating increased liability on
State Governments even in a phased manner would be acceptable to them. ( Para 9.2)
            The Committee notes that preparatory activities have been initiated in over 100 districts of more than 20
States/UTs.     Only one District Elementary  Education Plan has been received from Andhra Pradesh so far.   These
District Plans after their appraisal would be placed before the State and National level Mission for approval.   The
Committee is of the view that it would not be feasible to finish all these activities during  2001-2002. An allocation of
Rs.500 crores has been proposed for SSA for 2001-2002. The Committee observes that SSA has been under the
formulation stage since the beginning of Ninth Plan.  Allocations are being made every year showing nil expenditure at
the end of year. It was only during 2000-2001 that an expenditure of Rs.16.16 crore has been incurred upto 16.2.2001
against a BE provision of Rs. 350.00 crores apparently on preparatory activities prior to launching of SSA. In view of
the background, the Committee is of the view that Department should ensure that all the preparatory activities are
completed at the earliest leading to launching of the scheme already over-delayed. The Committee is of the considered
view that budgetary allocation for a scheme should be made only when the scheme has been finally approved. ( Para
9.3)
NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR WOMEN’S EDUCATION
            The Committee is constrained to note that the present status of the scheme is that its details are yet to be finalised
before other mandatory approvals, including approval of the Cabinet are sought. Allocation    and utilisation position of
funds is as follows:-

            The Committee is not convinced with the impact of Total Literacy Campaigns  as ground reality seems to be
entirely different, Under the banner of these campaigns, only processions of school children are being taken out.
Experience of Public representatives is that funds released for these campaigns are being misused by District
Collectors.   The Committee is of the opinion that Panchayats and Village Education Committees should also be
involved in this exercise.   Another suggestion is that instead of making TLC Volunteer-based, high school students can
be involved in the work of adult education.   The Committee has been informed that a panel of external evaluation
agencies has been drawn up who conduct the evaluation of the districts as per the norms and guidelines laid down by the
National Literacy Mission.   The Committee would like to be apprised about the findings of these reports, which at
present, are being summarized. (Para 16.2)
The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction with the trend of allocation and utilization of funds under different schemes
of Adult Education.  The Committee feels that the Scheme has totally failed in its objectives and there is no point in its
further continuance. (Para 16.3)
GENERAL

drastic reduction every year at the RE stage which the Committee feels is highly objectionable.  The Committee strongly
disapproves the tendency on the part of the Government to scuttle the entire Social Services Sector.  The Committee has
its own apprehension that drastic cut at the RE stage   is a deliberate attempt to save the funds for purposes best known
to the Government only.  The Committee is very unhappy about the entire approach.
