NEW DELHI;
April  12, 2001
Chaitra   22, 1923 (Saka)
 
 
S.B. CHAVAN
Chairman
Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on
Human Resource Development
REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION
1.1       Secondary Education marks a critical stage of education where process of transformation from childhood to
adulthood occurs.   In this phase children complete 10 years of basic education and 2 years of specialized education in
chosen fields including vocational stream.   It is the stage  where their knowledge and skills are tested for the first time
in public examinations conducted by various Boards.   It stands as a gateway to higher education for some and a stage
for entry into the world of work for others.
1.2       Higher Education, being at the apex of the educational pyramid,  has a key role to play in the education system.  
The National Policy on Education (NPE 1986)   visualizes higher education to be more dynamic and of high quality
because higher education   provides people an opportunity to reflect on the critical social, economic, cultural and
spiritual issues facing humanity.   Therefore, if the country has to make a progress, the importance of higher education
cannot be denied. 
II          BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The Secretary,  during the course of discussion,  stated that the Ninth Plan allocation of Rs. 7908.40 crore
against Rs. 3163.00 crore in the Eighth Five Year Plan is a positive step.   However, it still falls short of the projected
requirement of Rs. 15,589.77 crore.   The expenditure during the last four years was Rs. 5306.17 crore. Therefore, Rs.
2,602.23 crore should have been available for allocation in 2001-2002.  But actually, only Rs. 1920.00 crore under Plan
has been allocated for 2001-2002 against the projected requirement of Rs.3046.05 crore. Planning Commission has,
however, indicated that the allocation of additional funds will be made depending on the disinvestment process, it was
clarified.   The allocation in BE 2000-2001 was Rs. 1721.25 crore.   Therefore, there is an increase of 11.55% in 2001-
2002 as compared to the preceding year.   The allocation for Secondary Education in 2001-2002 is Rs. 648.00 crore as
against Rs. 600.00 crore in BE 2000-2001 which shows an increase of 8%. Similarly, for Higher Education Rs. 575.00
crore has been allocated in 2001-2002 as against Rs. 501.85 crore provided in last year, which shows an increase of
about 14.58%.   In the field of Technical Education, Rs. 575.00 crore has been allocated in 2001-2002 as against Rs.
500.00 crore  last year which is an escalation of 15%.  
2.2       The  Committee notes that Plan allocation of Rs. 1721.25 crore in BE 2000-2001 was  reduced to Rs. 1700.00
crore at the RE stage. The Department clarified that there has only been a marginal reduction in budget allocation  at RE
stage, mainly due to delay in revision of the Scheme of Computer Education in Schools (CLASS).
2.3       Contrary to the Plan allocation, the Committee observes that under Non-Plan, BE allocation in 2000-2001 was
Rs. 2930.09 crore which was enhanced to Rs. 3392.84 crore at the RE stage.  However, the BE allocation in 2001-2002
has been drastically reduced to  Rs. 2495.73 crore.  Asked as to the reason for this variation, the Department has
clarified that under  the Scheme of ‘Revision of Pay Scales of University and College Teachers’, Central Government is
to provide financial assistance to the State Governments for the period from 1.1.1996 to 31.3.2000 only to the extent of
80% of the additional expenditure involved in implementation of the Scheme.   An amount of Rs. 1511.80 crore has
already been released to the State Governments so far.  An amount of Rs. 600.00 crore was allocated for 2000-2001 for
disbursement to the State Governments.   This allocation was stepped up to Rs. 1060.00 crore at the RE stage keeping in
view the claims submitted/proposed to be submitted by the State Governments.  Since the claims of all the State
Governments were proposed to be settled in 2000-2001 the BE for 2001-2002 has been kept at Rs. 2.81 crore, as against
Rs. 600.00 crore provided last year.   However, some of the State Governments have not yet submitted their proposals in
the absence of which the RE is proposed to be kept at Rs. 825.00 crore.
2.4       The Committee has been given to understand that during 2001-2002,  vocationalisation of secondary education,
computer education in schools, revision of school curriculum, educational technology, expansion of Navodaya
Vidyalayas, quality upgradation in higher education sector, strengthening of distance mode of education, substantial
increase in the output of technical manpower, creation and augmentation of capacity in the field of information
technology, upgradation of Regional Engineering Colleges into world-class institutions, strengthening of national level
institutions like IITs, IIMs, IISc.  etc.   will be the major areas of priority.  

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/104threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:17]
2.5       The Committee observes that the projected requirement of the Department during Ninth Plan was Rs. 15,589.77
crore.  During all the five years of Ninth Plan, trend of allocation of funds has been below the requirements as projected
by the Department.  The Committee is constrained to observe that during the first four years of Ninth Plan, allocations
have been invariably reduced at the RE stage substantially or marginally and  even this reduced provision continued to
be under utilized except during 1999-2000.  The Committee notes that against the RE allocation of Rs. 1700.00 crore in
2000-2001, expenditure reported upto 16.2.2001, is only Rs. 1179.97 crore.  The Committee is, therefore, of the view
that the Department should make concerted efforts for optimum utilisation of allocated funds in accordance with the
physical and financial targets set for different schemes of both secondary and higher education.
III        NATIONAL COUNCIL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH & TRAINING (NCERT)
3.1       Plan allocation for NCERT in 2000-2001 was Rs.13.00 crore which was reduced to Rs.10.00 crore at the RE
stage and allocation in BE 2001-2002 is Rs.11.20 crore which is still less than last year’s BE allocation. The Department
has clarified that the Plan allocation of NCERT was reduced last year at RE stage from Rs. 13.00 crore to  Rs. 10.00
crore as NCERT had an unspent balance of Rs.2.83 crore as on 1.4.2000. Against the projected demand of Rs. 13.00
crore for 2001-2002, the Planning Division of the Department reduced this to Rs.11.20 crore. 
3.2       The Committee has been informed that the NCERT has completed the review of the 10 year old National
Curriculum Framework and has brought out the National Curriculum Framework during November, 2000 which has
been circulated to all the State Governments/UTs and Boards etc. for further consideration.  It was clarified that a
discussion document on National Curriculum Framework was released in January, 2000 and was sent to all the State
Education Ministers, Chairman of Boards of School Education, Directors of SCERTs, NGOs etc. for their comments
and suggestions.   Regional Seminars were also organized to discuss the draft document in different   States.   The
document was also placed before Governing Body of the NCERT in which all the State Governments. are represented
through their respective Education Ministers.   The Committee was given to understand that about 12-13 State
Education Ministers participated in this meeting.   NCERT is also planning to conduct meetings in different States in
this issue and one meeting has already been held in Tripura.   The Committee desires that a meeting of Central Advisory
Board on Education (CABE) may also be convened by the Department on this issue.   
IV        KENDIRIYA VIDALAYA SANGATHAN (KVS)
4.1       BE allocation for the year 1999-2000 for Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan was Rs.544.81 crore which got
enhanced to Rs.590.59 crore in 2000-2001 Non Plan allocation of Rs.454.81 crore enhanced to Rs.495.59 crore in 2000-
2001  was primarily meant for meeting the expenditure on pay and allowances, retirement benefits and cost of essential
services.  Plan allocation was enhanced to Rs.95.00 crore in 2000-2001 against an allocation  Rs.90.00 crore in 1999-
2000 for maintenance and repairs of school buildings affected by severe cyclone in Orissa. However, the Committee has
been informed that only a small amount of Plan funds i.e.  Rs.4.57 lakhs was required for carrying out special repairs of
school buildings and staff quarters affected by the cyclone in Ganjam District of Orissa on 17.10.1999 which was
sanctioned by KVS in May, 2000.
4.2       The cyclone affected the coastal Districts of Orissa, particularly Ganjam, Balasore, Bhadrak, Cuttack, Puri,
Khurda, Dhenkanal, Kendrapara and other places from 28/10/1999 onwards.  The Committee is, however, perturbed to
note that  only a small amount has been sanctioned for Ganjam District alone and that too only  in May, 2000 i.e after 6-
7 months.  The Committee wonders whether no damage was caused to the KV School Buildings in any of the costal
districts of Orissa due to the cyclone.  In case, there were other school buildings affected by the  cyclone, funds should
have been sanctioned and released for their construction/repairs.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the
number of KVS functioning in  Orissa (district wise) and status of schools damaged by the cyclone in 1999.
4.3       Last year, the Committee was given to understand that construction work was in progress in 79 KV Schools.   
The Committee observes that out of the 79 Kendriya Vidyalayas, construction works have been completed in respect of 
KV, Leh and KV No.1, Itanagar. As per the latest information, buildings plans are under preparation/processing for 73
KVS.  The  Committee expresses its dissatisfaction over the slow progress of construction works of KVs.  The
Committee recommends that there should be proper monitoring of construction works of the KVS so as to complete the
projects in a fixed time frame.
V         NAVODAYA VIDYALAYA SAMITI (NVS)
5.1       The Committee was informed that 94 Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas (JNVs) were to be opened during Ninth
Plan.  These Vidyalayas are initially started in temporary accommodation provided by the State Governments.  58
Vidyalayas have already been sanctioned and rest of the Vidyalayas are expected to be covered  during 2001-2002.  It
has also been  informed that out of the 440 Vidyalayas sanctioned so far, construction of buildings has been sanctioned
for 380 Vidyalayas.  Out of this, 286 Vidyalayas are functioning in their own buildings with the construction of
buildings of 158 Vidyalayas having been completed and buildings of 128 Vidyalayas are in advanced stage of

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/104threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:17]
completion. 
5.2       The Committee notes that out of 94 JNVs to be opened during the Ninth Plan, 58 JNVs have already been
sanctioned and the remaining 36 JNVs are expected to be sanctioned during 2001-2002, i.e. the last year of the Ninth
Plan.  The Committee hopes that the Department would be able to achieve its target of opening JNVs during the Ninth
Plan.  The Committee also notes that construction work of 128 JNVs is in advanced stage.  The committee recommends
the  completion of all these school buildings by the end of Ninth Plan through constant monitoring.
5.3       The Committee has been informed that there are 60 JNVs for which the assured land has not yet been transferred
by the State Governments.   The concerned States are Arunanchal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chattisgarh, Gujarat,
Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Orissa, Punjab,
Sikkim, Uttar Pradesh and Uttranchal.  There are 115 JNVs where the sanctioned strength of 80 students each class is
not being maintained due to shortage of accommodation.  This is because of the fact that in some cases, due to non-
provision of adequate temporary accommodation, the level of intake has to be restricted. 
5.4       The Committee is constrained to observe that a number of states have not transferred the land for construction of
JNVs, as assured by them, with the result construction of as many as 60 schools could not be undertaken.  The
Committee, therefore, feels that the Department should pursue the matter with the concerned State Governments, even
at the higher level if necessary,  so that land is made available for construction of  buildings for JNVS.
 VI       VOCATIONALISATION OF EDUCATION
6.1       The Department has informed that the Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Vocationalisation of Education has so far
created 19,455 sections in 6728 schools, thus providing diversion of over 10 lakh students at +2 level.  So far Rs. 645.98
crore have been released.  Most of the states have shown progress in implementation of the scheme.     
6.2       Budget provision for this scheme in 1999-2000 and 2000-2001 was Rs.10.5 crore, and Rs.35.00 crore
respectively, Rs.42.70 crore has been allocated for 2001-2002.   The Department has informed that in order to
accommodate the demand of the States for expansion of the Vocational Education Scheme, the RE allocation for 2000-
2001 was enhanced to Rs.45.00 crore.  However, the Committee is constrained to observe that expenditure reported upto
16.2.2001 is only Rs. 30.74 crore which is even less than the BE allocation of Rs. 35.00 crore.
6.3       What is more disturbing is that during the years 1999-2000 and 2000-01, no grants were released to Andhra
Pradesh, Arunchal Pradesh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, J&K, Orissa, Punjab, Sikkim & Tripura.  Moreover, funds
allocated to various States have decreased drastically as compared to the earlier allocations. It is also not known whether
this scheme is in operation in States/UTs of Meghalaya, A & N Islands, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Daman and Diu and
Lakshadweep.
6.4       Delay in starting the construction of Pt. Sunderlal Sharma Central Institute of Vocational Education (PSSCIVE),
Bhopal in 1993 has been engaging the attention of the Committee for quite some time.  As per the latest information
made available to the Committee, the rough cost estimates  have been prepared by the School of Planning and
Architecture after the final selection of the site.  NCERT has been asked to confirm that the space requirements are as
per the norms following which the proposal will be put up to SFC/EFC for necessary approval after obtaining the
estimates from the CPWD.  The Committee is of the view that all procedural formalities should be expedited and funds
allocated so that construction of the building of PSSCIVE, Bhopal is started at the earliest.
VII       COMPUTER EDUCATION IN SCHOOLS, [ERSTWHILE SCHEME OF COMPUTER LITERACY AND
STUDIES IN SCHOOLS (CLASS)]
7.1       A pilot project on Computer Literacy and Studies in Schools (CLASS) was initiated in 1984-85.  The project
continued upto 1992-93 on adhoc basis.  The implementation of CLASS project was then reviewed by C&AG.  The
C+AG report identified multiplicity of agencies, diffused responsibility and inadequate monitoring etc.  Accordingly, a
modified scheme was prepared and introduced from 1993-94 which continued to be implemented as a Centrally
Sponsored Scheme upto 1999.  2371 schools were covered under the modified scheme during Eighth Plan.  However, in
the meanwhile, on the advice of the Ministry of Finance, it was decided that the scheme be phased out and only
maintenance funds were to be released to States/UTs.  All the State Govts/UT Administrations were, accordingly, 
informed about the discontinuance of the scheme  from 1.4.99.      
7.2       The latest position is that a revised scheme in place of erstwhile Computer Literacy and Studies in School
(CLASS) Scheme is in an advanced stage of formulation and is expected to be operationalised during 2001-2002.  
When asked about the necessity of revising the scheme, the Department has stated that the very nature of the erstwhile
scheme was “Supply driven”  and there was little involvement of teachers and students with the scheme.  Therefore, the
progress of the scheme remained slow.   In the new scheme, attempts have been made to correct these shortcomings. 
The Committee has been further informed that the proposed scheme would not be a `stand alone’ scheme and would aim
at  capturing the developments which are taking place  in the field of IT Education in various States.   The revised

REPORT

scheme would be posited within the overall environment in each State in which diverse measures for imparting IT

VIII      INTEGRATED EDUCATION FOR DISABLED CHILDREN (IEDC)
8.1       The Scheme of Integrated Education for Disabled Children (IEDC) is presently being implemented in 27 states
and 5 UTs with over 22,000 schools benefiting  more than 95,000 disabled children.  The scheme is being implemented
by State Govts. as well as NGOs.
8.2       The Committee has been informed that the financial outlay for IEDC scheme in the Ninth Plan period is Rs.100
crore.  During the first four years of the Ninth Plan, about Rs.46.69 crore have been spent in the implementation of the
scheme.  The BE allocation for 2001-2002 has been kept at Rs.21.40 cores.  The Committee is  constrained to observe 
that the allocation for the Ninth Plan for the Scheme will not be fully utilized, giving an impression that the
implementations of the Scheme is not satisfactory.
8.3       As per the details of students/schools covered under the scheme upto 1999-2000, Goa, Meghalaya, Sikkim, J &K
and UT  of Chandigarh do not seem to be participating at all.  In contrast, in States like Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat,
Orissa, Tamil Nadu and Haryana, both State Govts. and NGOs are actively involved.  The Committee observes that in
West Bengal whereas it seems every year new school is being taken up by State Govt. for implementation of the
scheme, 169 students in 81 schools have been covered upto 1999-2000 by 2 NGOs.  Case of UP seems to be even
worse.  Grants released for 32 schools (figures of students not available) are lying unspent for long.  In contrast, 6
NGOs are managing 667 students in 265 schools.  The Scheme of Integrated Education for the Disabled Children
(IEDC) launched in 1974 has undergone two revisions, so far.  The Committee is, however, perturbed to note that the
scheme is not being implemented properly due to non-availability of infrastructure/financial assistance/specially
qualified teachers with States/UTs.
8.4       Last year, the Committee  was informed that NCERT had been requested to conduct an impact study with a view
of ascertaining the impact of the IEDC Scheme.  It seems that not much progress has been made by NCERT in this
matter.  The Committee is of the view that this study should be expedited by NCERT.  The Committee would also like
to emphasise that there is an urgent need for having an effective monitoring mechanism for this scheme.

12.1     Under the Scheme ‘Strengthening of  Boarding/Hostel Facilities for Girl students of Secondary and Higher

construction of hostels and for revision of rates for recurring items was continuing.    The Committee observes that the

XVIII   TECHNICAL EDUCATION
The Committee observes that Information Technology is in much demand in the present context. This has given rise to a
situation where greater and greater number of students are opting for it  at the cost of other branches of engineering.   IT
is developing at the cost of other core areas like Civil Engineering and Pure Research. This may in future create a
situation when we would be having surplus of IT students and deficiency in other branches of engineering  Therefore, a
proper planning  is imperative for a balanced growth.

XXII    GENERAL
22.1     The Committee over the years has observed that a higher provision is generally made in the BE which is
subsequently reduced at RE stage. The actual expenditure is even less due to one reason or the other.  The Committee
strongly feels that a new scheme should not be reflected in the Budget, unless its feasibility has been fully examined and
it has been finally approved. Tenth Plan is to commence from 2002-2003.   The Committee is of the view that it should
be ensured that no scheme is launched and budget provisions made therefor during the period without proper scrutiny.  
Similarly, exercise of revision of a particular scheme should be completed within the shortest period possible so that
reduction in the allocation of funds is not resorted to at the RE stage for two-three years on a continuous basis.
22.2     The entire approach seems to be adhoc and the intention seems to be a deliberate attempt not to implement the
educational policies under one pretext or the other and the Finance Ministry is giving  an impression of making an
impressive provision at the BE and drastically reducing the same at RE stage and even this reduce provision is not
spent.   The Committee is getting an impression that without resources Government wants merely to announce the
Schemes and are interested in saving the funds for the purpose unknown to the Committee.

REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION
1.1       The development of women and children to their full potential is an essential component in the country’s total
human resource development.  In its capacity as a nodal agency looking after the advancement of women and children,
the Department of Women & Child Development formulates plans, policies and programmes, enacts/amends legislation
affecting women and children and guides and coordinates the efforts of both Governmental and non-Governmental
organizations working in the field of Women and Child Development.   Apart from this, the Department also
implements certain innovative programmes for women and children in the areas of employment and income generation,
welfare and support services, gender sensitization, training for employment and income generation and awareness
generation.  All these efforts are directed to ensure that women are empowered both economically and socially and thus
become equal partners in national development alongwith men.
1.2       For a holistic child development, the Department implements the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)
which provides an integrated package of services comprising supplementary nutrition, immunization, health check-up
and pre-school and non-formal education and health and nutrition education.  The ultimate objective of all these
programmes is to ensure that children grow and live in a healthy and secure environment.
II         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       Total outlay for the Department during Ninth Plan is Rs.7810.42 crores. Plan allocation for 2001-2002, the last
year of Ninth Plan is Rs.1650.00 crores which represents a step-up of 22.2% over the RE allocation of previous year
(Rs.1350.00 crores). The Committee has been informed that this increase does not match the projected demand of the
Department which was Rs.2776.79 crore. Higher allocation was required for expanding the existing programmes and
also for starting new programmes, i.e. National Nutrition Mission, new schemes for women during the Women’s
Empowerment Year. However, due to lesser allocation, the Department has to restrict its programmes within the
available funds.
2.2       The Committee observes that during 2000-2001 also although the Department had projected a requirement of
Rs.2034.14 crore, an amount of only Rs.1460.00 crore was made available which was reduced to Rs.1350.00 crore at
the RE stage. What is more disturbing is that expenditure reported upto 13.3.2001 is only Rs.1199.67 crore. Situation
was virtually the same during 1998-99 and 1999-2000. The Committee had pointed out that maximum level of
expenditure during 1998-99 was in the month of March (against a total plan expenditure at Rs.1131.84 crore, figures for
March stood at Rs.474.52 crores) The Committee has noticed that there has been slight improvement during 1999-2000.
Against RE  allocation of Rs.1249.86 crore, expenditure reported upto 31.1.2000 was Rs.998.34 crore which went up to
Rs.1244.79 crore by the end of financial year i.e. 31.3.2000.
2.3       The Committee has been informed that in order to spread out the expenditure throughout the year, regular review
meetings were undertaken at various levels in the Department. Frequency of the meetings of the Project Sanctioning
Committee was also increased for expeditious clearance of the projects. The Committee is, however, constrained to
observe that these corrective measures have not proved to be of much help as large gaps still continued between the
issuance of the sanctions and the actual release of fund due to the following reasons:-
non-submission of utlisation certificates by NGOs and State Governments.
Non-furnishing of Pre-Stamped Receipts (PSR) and the Bonds duly signed by the recipient organizations, despite
repeated reminders.
The Committee views this with serious concern. The Committee recommends that the Department should vigorously
pursue fulfilment of required conditions both with the defaulter NGOs and States. The Committee is of the view that
stringent action needs to be taken against such NGOs and further grant should not be released in case of non-submission

of utilisation certificates by implementing agencies. Department’s responsibility does not end with sending reminders.
Fact finding teams should be sent in case of chronic defaulters so that real picture about the functioning of a particular
scheme can emerge.
III        INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS) (GENERAL)
3.1       The ICDS Scheme aims at providing an integrated package of services to the children below 6 years, pregnant
women and nursing mothers. The services include supplementary nutrition, immunization health check-up, referral
services, pre-school and non-formal education and health and nutrition education. The Scheme is a centrally sponsored
scheme with funds allocated to State Governments/UT Administrations for delivery of services at grass root Anganwadi
Centres. At present the scheme is operational in 4384 blocks and expected to cover 4550 blocks by March, 2001 and
5171 blocks by March, 2002.
3.2       The allocation of ICDS for 2001-2002 is Rs.1198.00 crore against a requirement of Rs.1307.00 crore.  Last year,
the Committee was informed that under the revised ICDS Scheme, 10 Mini Anganwadi Centres can be opened in lieu of
a full-fledged Anganwadi so that small hamlets/villages in tribal blocks having less than 300 population and situated in
far-flung areas can be accommodated. The Committee notes that proposals for opening of 21,1017 and 80 mini-
Anganwadi Centres have been received from Mizoram, Manipur and Assam respectively, which are under consideration
of the Department.  The Committee recommends that required procedural formalities should be expedited so that these
mini-Anganwadi Centres are opened at the earliest. The Department should also pursue other concerned state
Governments in this regard.
3.3       It has been reported that various studies have proved the efficacy of ICDS Scheme with reference to its impact
on Infant Mortality Rate. As per the figures about 17 States made available to the Committee, IMR among the ICDS
beneficiaries has been found to be significantly lower in comparison with general population as per the Sample
Registration Survey (SRS) (1998), National Family Health Survey-II (1998-99) and National Council of Applied
Economic Research (NCAER) (2000-2001). While inclined to agree with the reported figures, the Committee is
perturbed to note that situation is quite alarming in the two major States as indicated below-

incidence of malnutrition deaths in tribal areas. Eleven States/UTs which include Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh,
Meghalaya, J & K, Orissa, Dadra & Nagar Haveli have prepared Plan of Action. Another important measure initiated is
Areas Officers designated by the Department for various States/group of States to concentrate on tribal areas during
their visits. An inter-ministerial fact finding team was also sent by the Department to those areas where such incidents
have been reported.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the assessment made by Area Officers/Inter-
ministerial teams and also corrective measures initiated as a follow-up.
3.5       Nutrition is an important component of the package of services offered under ICDS.  The expenditure towards
supplementary feeding is met by the State under the Plan budget, available for Minimum Needs Programme. However,
in view of required provision not being made by most of the States due to their resource constraints, an additional
allocation of Rs.375.00 crore was provided by the Department during 2000-2001 under Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya
Yojana (PMGY).  The Committee is dismayed to note that non-contribution of sufficient counterpart funds for Nutrition
Component or due to lesser allocation of funds in the Plan/Non-Plan budget or in some cases diversion of funds
allocated for SNP to some other schemes has led to a situation where there is a large gap in the availability of funds and
requirement of funds which has caused interruptions in the delivery of this vital input.

be interested to know whether the aforesaid Committee had recommended enhancement of honorarium to
AWWs/Helpers. The Committee finds that 14 States/UTs are providing additional honorarium to AWWs/Helpers. 
However, major States in view of their poor financial position have failed to take any initiative in this regard and there
are little chances of their doing so in future. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation for
enhancement of honorarium to AWWs/Helpers.
3.9       A field survey of nearly 60,000 Anganwadi Centres and 1,80,000 beneficiary households selected from 4000
operational blocks (as on 31.3.1996) spread over 32 States/UTs has been conducted by NCAER. The Committee notes
that major findings of this study are as follows:-
although most AWCs located within a distance of 100-200 metres from the beneficiary households, coverage of
programme limited to over 50% eligible children and women.
Only about 36%, AWCs housed in pucca buildings.
Less than 25%, of AWCs reporting toilet facility in majority of the States.
Adequate staffing of AWCs.
Inadequate availability of inventories.
Inadequate provision of in-service training.
Limited convergence and co-operation both within and between the departments of ICDS
Lukewarm support from community.
The Committee observes that performance of West Bengal, Punjab, J & K, U.P. and Bihar has been reported to be
below average. The Committee recommends that the Department should keep on monitoring the ICDS activities,
specially in weaker States and initiate adequate measures for removal of bottlenecks/constraints.
IV        WORLD BANK ASSISTED ICDS
World Bank provides credit to centrally sponsored ICDS Projects. During 2000-2001, a provision of Rs.180.00 crore
was made for implementation of ICDS-II Project in Bihar, M.P., Chattisgarh, Jharkhand and A.P. and ICDS-III Project
in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Maharasthra, U.P. and Rajasthan. However, this provision was reduced to Rs.140.00 crore at the
RE stage.  Besides other reasons, the States  being not in a position to utilise all the funds due to carry-over balance of
earlier years has been cited as the main reason.   The Committee views with concern an expenditure of only Rs.48.00
crore upto 15.1.2001. Latest figures  reveal reported expenditure of Rs.105.88 crore upto 13.3.2001. The Committee is
not satisfied with the uneven spread of expenditure Rs.57.88 crore seem to have been spent in a period of two months
against an expenditure of Rs.48.00 crore in more than nine months. The Committee recommends that the Department
should initiate remedial measures at the earliest in view of proposed enhanced allocation of Rs.220.00 crores under
World Bank Assisted ICDS in 2001-2002.
V         TRAINING PROGRAMME UNDER ICDS (UDISHA)
5.1       World Bank assisted training programme under ICDS ‘UDISHA’ has an outlay of Rs.600.00 crores over a five
year period from 1999-2000 to 2003-2004. It envisages the upward revision of financial norms, integration and co-
ordination of training of ICDS functionaries and revision of training syllabus.
5.2       The Department has informed that due to lack of understanding of the World Bank Accounting Procedures, there
was delay in submission of Reimbursement Claims by State Governments/UTs in the initial years.  However, with

VI        CRECHES/DAY CARE CENTRES FOR CHILDREN OF WORKING MOTHERS/AILING MOTHERS
6.1       The Scheme is being implemented by Central Social Welfare Board (CSWB) through voluntary Social Welfare
Organisations and by two other national level organizations, namely, Indian Council for Child Welfare (ICCW) and
Bhartiya Adim Jati Sevak Sangh (BAJSS). 12,470 Creche units are being run covering around 3.11 lakh beneficiaries.
6.2       Last year, the Committee had noticed that due to unspent balances available with the implementing agencies as
on 1.4.99, budget provision of Rs.20.50 crore was reduced to Rs.17.00 crore at the RE stage. An amount of Rs.15.49
crore was utilised upto 31.3.2000. The Committee finds that situation has not improved during 2000-2001. A lower
provision of Rs.18.50 crore was made due to unspent balances of about Rs.4.00 crore available with CSWB. Funds
released upto 13.3.2001 is Rs.10.74 crore.
6.3       The Committee takes serious view of the fact that major unspent balances are with CSWB. Out of total 12,470
Creches being run, CSWB is handling 9364 Creches. Besides that, 374 creches have been withheld by CSWB, reasons
for which are not known to the Committee. The Committee would like to have full details about these crèches, statewise
alongwith action taken by CSWB so far. The Committee, in view of the fact that higher allocation of Rs.21`.95 crores is
proposed for 2001-2002, would also like to be apprised about the other alternatives contemplated by the Department in
the event of CSWB failing in full utilisation of funds.
VII       CONDENSED COURSES OF EDUCATION FOR ADULT WOMEN
7.1       Under this scheme, grant is given to NGOs for conducting courses of two year duration for preparing candidates
for primary, middle and matric level examinations and one year duration for matric-failed candidates.
7.2       The Committee has been informed that an unspent balance of Rs.6.36 crores was available with CSWB as on
31.3.2000. Decision to consider grant for Middle and Higher level courses to only those NGOs engaged in educational
activities led to reduced number of eligible organizations resulting in release of only Rs.12.95 lakhs for 60 courses
during initial months of 1999-2000. However, as per a decision taken on 20.7.2000, institutions engaged in women
welfare activities (as being done earlier) were also considered for funding. As a result, during the period (July-
Dec.,2000), more than 200 courses were sanctioned and Rs.1.50 crores utilised.
7.3       The Committee observes that against an allocation of Rs.1.50 crores under ‘Condensed Courses for Women
Education’, expenditure figures upto 13.3.2001 are shown as only Rs.18.00 lakhs. The Committee feels that unspent
balances were adjusted during 2000-2001 also. This is borne out by the fact that due to non-appointment of regular
Chairpersons in some of the State Boards, regular work suffered resulting in non-settlement of their accounts. All the
State Boards have now been directed by CSWB to settle the accounts of NGOs on priority basis so that past liabilities
may be cleared and unspent balances, if any, may be adjusted in further releases. The Committee would like to be
enlightened about the progress made in this matter. The Committee strongly feels that accounting procedure for this
programme requires to be made fool-proof and transparent. On no account unspent balances should be allowed to be
lying with the implementing agencies, be it CSWB/State Boards/NGOs. The Committee is of the view that the scheme
of ‘Condensed Courses of Education for Adult Women’ needs to be evaluated by an independent agency. Achievements
made by candidates prepared under this scheme in primary, middle and matric level examination should be a component
of this evaluation.

8.1       Balika Samridh Yojana covers upto two girl children born on or after 15  August, 1997 in a Below Priority Line

name of the girl child. In addition, the girl child will be entitled to receive scholarship for each class of study ranging
from Rs.300/- for Class I to Rs.1000/- for Class X which will also be deposited in the above account. Scheme is being
implemented through ICDS infrastructure and in non-ICDS areas through district level agencies.
8.2       The Committee notes that allocation of Rs.27.00 crores in 2000-2001 was reduced to Rs.21.00 crore at RE stage
due to slow pace of utilisation of funds by States/UTs during the earlier years. The Committee is, however, perturbed to
observe that an expenditure of only Rs.13.43 crore has been incurred upto 13.3.2001. Achievement level of Physical
Targets is also very discouraging. Only 2.70 lakhs beneficiaries have been reported against a target of 12 lakh
beneficiaries.
8.3       The Committee is shocked to learn that since 1997-98, an amount of Rs.169.66 crores has been released to all
the States/UTs. Fund utilisation position is as low as Rs.49.02 crores (31.41% of total allocation).  Details made
available to the Committee clearly indicate that all the States/UTs with the exception of Punjab, Mizoram, Tripura,

procedure. There are States which have failed to submit utilisation certificates from the first year onwards. Funds,

IX        HOSTELS FOR WORKING WOMEN
9.1       The objective of the scheme is to provide cheap and safe hostel accommodation to working women, women
getting training for employment and girl students studying in post school professional courses.  Allocation of Rs. 9.00
crore has been proposed for 2001-2002.  The Committee notes with concern that there has been an expenditure of only
Rs.4.81 crores upto 13.3.2001 against an allocation of Rs. 7.02 crores during 2000-2001.  There has been shortfall in
achievement of Physical Targets also.   Only 1275 beneficiaries have been reported against a target of 2500
beneficiaries.  The Committee is dismayed to find that out of 861 hostels sanctioned, only 613 hostels have been
completed so far.  248 hostels are incomplete which include cases where assistance upto 90% has been released.  The
Committee is shocked to learn that response is still awaited from the concerned State Governments  about status
position of Working Women Hostels asked for by the Department in September, 1999, followed by reminders in
November, 1999 and November, 2000.  The Committee feels that the matter should be taken up at a higher level. 
9.2       Instances have also come to the notice of the Committee that in some States Working Women Hostels are not
functioning well.  All types of complaints are there against them.  The Committee hopes that Area Officers designated
by the Department, besides pursuing the cases of incomplete hostels, would also look into such complaints.  Ideal
position would be if a mechanism can be evolved whereby area MP/MLA is also involved in such exercises.
X         SHORT STAY HOMES
10.1     Under this scheme, grants-in-aid are given to Voluntary Organisations for establishing and running Short Stay
Homes for rehabilitating women and girls, facing social and moral danger.  The recurring cost as per the changed norms
is Rs. 4,01,350 per Home per annum in `C’ class city with a one time non-recurring grant of Rs. 50,000.  The work of

new Homes continues to be the responsibility of the Department.  At present, there are 339 SSHs , out of which 120
SSHs were sanctioned during 2000-2001 including 51 for earthquake affected areas of Gujarat.
10.2     The Committee had noticed that in 1997-98 and 1998-99, actual expenditure was less than the revised estimates
on account of lower releases to NGOs due to unspent balances  available with them.  During 1999-2000 also there was
under utilization of funds due to mainly unsatisfactory performance reports from some of the Homes and also non-

BE allocation of Rs. 12.00 crore was reduced to Rs. 8.00 crore and expenditure reported upto 13.3.2001 is only Rs. 2.13
crore.  It seems that out of 120 SSHs  sanctioned during 2000-2001, majority of them still continue to remain sanctioned
on paper.  The Committee is of the view that revision of the scheme based on evaluation done in 1997-98 by
Programme Evaluation Organisation of Planning Commission has not led to better performance.
10.3     The Committee has been given to understand that besides regular inspections by State Board Officials, surprise
and regular visits are also being made by CSWB officials and also Area Officers of the Department.  The Committee is,
however not inclined to have much faith in these inspections as adverse reports continue to keep on coming to the notice
of public representatives.  The Committee feels that involvement of local MPs/MLAs in inspections, to the extent
possible is required so as to have the actual assessment of ground realities.
XI        SUPPORT TO TRAINING AND EMPLOYMENT PROGRAMME (STEP)
11.1     The programme, launched in 1986-87, consists of a series of action-oriented projects intended to enhance the
productivity and income-generation of women in the traditional sectors such as agriculture, animal husbandry, dairying,
fisheries, handlooms, handicrafts etc.  Women beneficiaries are organized into viable and cohesive groups or co-
operatives.  The Programme is implemented through Public Sector Undertakings and Voluntary Agencies.  Since, the
inception of the Programme, about 4, 91, 795 women have been covered under 96 projects launched in the states of AP,
Bihar, Gujarat, Haryana, HP, Kerala, Karnataka, Orissa, MP, Maharashtra, Manipur, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, UP and West
Bengal.
11.2     Under this programme the plan allocation has been increased from Rs.13.00 crores in 2000-2001 to Rs.18.00
crores in 2001-2002.  Justifying the increase ,the Department has stated that the number of projects being received and
approved has increased to a great extent as compared to previous years.  The allocation will be utilized for sanctioning
of new projects and giving instalments for second and third year of the projects sanctioned in the previous years.
11.3     The Committee notes that an expenditure of Rs. 9.13 crore has been reported upto 13.3.2001 against an
allocation of Rs. 13.00 crore.  The Committee has been informed that under the scheme, about 70% of the projects
implemented so far have been in the dairy sector and there are more than 6000 women’s dairy co-operatives in the
country now.  While appreciating the impact of STEP on dairy farming initiatives taken by women, the Committee feels
that women should be encouraged to involve themselves in other sectors like animal husbandry, fisheries, handlooms,
handicrafts, khadi and village industries, sericulture etc.  as envisaged under this programme.
XII       SOCIO- ECONOMIC PROGRAMME
12.1     Under this programme, initiated in 1958, NGOs are given financial assistance for providing economic
rehabilitation to the poor and disabled women by providing avenues for full time or part time work through production
units, dairy units and self-employment schemes.  Against a provision of Rs. 1.00 crore in 2000-2001, no expenditure has
been incurred upto 13.3.2001.  However, the Committee has been given to understand that two NGOs were provided
assistance with  a sum of Rs. 0.64 lakhs and also Rs. 33.06 lakhs were given to State Boards for arranging exhibition of
the products of NGOs.
12.2     The Committee has been given to understand that following decisions taken by CSWB during 1997-98 can be
held to be responsible for non-achievement of financial and physical targets under this programme during the period
1997-2000:-
Sanction of grants to only those organisations having women as members of the Managing Committee.
Proposals under Production Unit recommended by the State Boards to be sent to NIESBUD for further scrutiny.
            However, as a result of subsequent decision taken by CSWB in December, 2000, the above mentioned
conditions have been withdrawn and the earlier conditions as prevailing before 1997-98 are in force.
12.3     The Committee is not convinced with the reversion to original schematic pattern of the programme due to
sufficient number of proposals not forthcoming from NGOs having women members.  The Committee is also not in
agreement with the  decision of not sending the proposals under Production Unit cleared by State Boards to NIESBUD
for further scrutiny.  Inspite of efforts made by CSWB at various levels, as many as 3390 NGOs still remain blacklisted
on ground of non-submission of accounts and failure to refund the loan amount.  Not only this, State Boards of Gujarat,

13.1     The Rashtriya Mahila Kosh (RMK) has been given a one time corpus of Rs. 31.00 crore which is being used as a
revolving fund to provide loans to poor women mainly through NGOs  well versed in credit management.  It also
channelises loans through women development corporations and co-operative societies.  The Committee has been
informed that since its inception on 30.3.93, upto 31
st January, 2001, RMK has been able to sanction credit limits of Rs.
94.54 crore through 820 NGOs to benefit 3,93,345 women.  The Committee observes that out of Rs. 94.54 crore

13.2     Last year the Committee was informed that the total provision in 1999-2000 would remain unutilised as the EFC

there has been virtually no progress during 2000-2001 as the proposal still remained to be finalized and no expenditure
against an allocation of Rs. 3.00 crore has been incurred upto 13.3.2001.  The Committee finds that during 2001-2002
also in view of uncertainly about approval of the proposal for augmentation of corpus  funds, a provision of only Rs.
1.00 crore has been proposed. The Committee fails to understand the reasons for undue delay in taking a final decision

XVI     NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR WOMEN
16.1     The National Commission for Women has the mandate to safeguard the rights and interests of women and to
review all Central and State laws relating to or affecting women.  It also receives petitions from women for redressal of
their grievances.  The Committee has been informed that a higher provision of Rs. 5.00 crore has been made in 2001-
2002 for activities to be undertaken as part of Women’s Empowerment Year, 2001 and for additional sanctioned posts.
16.2     The Committee notes that NCW received 5268 complaints during 2000 which were referred to the concerned
State Women Commissions/State Departments where State Women Commissions are not established.  The Committee
was given to understand that inquiries conducted by NCW do not have the desired impact due to lack of powers given to
NCW at present.  The Committee notes that there is a proposal to enhance the powers of the Commission as given to

like to be apprised about the procedure for selection of members of NCW.

remove provisions discriminatory to women.  So far 21 legislations have been reviewed by NCW.  The Committee

REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION
1.1       Secondary Education marks a critical stage of education where process of transformation from childhood to
adulthood occurs.   In this phase children complete 10 years of basic education and 2 years of specialized education in
chosen fields including vocational stream.   It is the stage  where their knowledge and skills are tested for the first time
in public examinations conducted by various Boards.   It stands as a gateway to higher education for some and a stage
for entry into the world of work for others.
1.2       Higher Education, being at the apex of the educational pyramid,  has a key role to play in the education system.  
The National Policy on Education (NPE 1986)   visualizes higher education to be more dynamic and of high quality
because higher education   provides people an opportunity to reflect on the critical social, economic, cultural and
spiritual issues facing humanity.   Therefore, if the country has to make a progress, the importance of higher education
cannot be denied. 
II          BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The Secretary,  during the course of discussion,  stated that the Ninth Plan allocation of Rs. 7908.40 crore
against Rs. 3163.00 crore in the Eighth Five Year Plan is a positive step.   However, it still falls short of the projected
requirement of Rs. 15,589.77 crore.   The expenditure during the last four years was Rs. 5306.17 crore. Therefore, Rs.
2,602.23 crore should have been available for allocation in 2001-2002.  But actually, only Rs. 1920.00 crore under Plan
has been allocated for 2001-2002 against the projected requirement of Rs.3046.05 crore. Planning Commission has,
however, indicated that the allocation of additional funds will be made depending on the disinvestment process, it was
clarified.   The allocation in BE 2000-2001 was Rs. 1721.25 crore.   Therefore, there is an increase of 11.55% in 2001-
2002 as compared to the preceding year.   The allocation for Secondary Education in 2001-2002 is Rs. 648.00 crore as
against Rs. 600.00 crore in BE 2000-2001 which shows an increase of 8%. Similarly, for Higher Education Rs. 575.00
crore has been allocated in 2001-2002 as against Rs. 501.85 crore provided in last year, which shows an increase of
about 14.58%.   In the field of Technical Education, Rs. 575.00 crore has been allocated in 2001-2002 as against Rs.
500.00 crore  last year which is an escalation of 15%.  
2.2       The  Committee notes that Plan allocation of Rs. 1721.25 crore in BE 2000-2001 was  reduced to Rs. 1700.00
crore at the RE stage. The Department clarified that there has only been a marginal reduction in budget allocation  at RE
stage, mainly due to delay in revision of the Scheme of Computer Education in Schools (CLASS).
2.3       Contrary to the Plan allocation, the Committee observes that under Non-Plan, BE allocation in 2000-2001 was
Rs. 2930.09 crore which was enhanced to Rs. 3392.84 crore at the RE stage.  However, the BE allocation in 2001-2002
has been drastically reduced to  Rs. 2495.73 crore.  Asked as to the reason for this variation, the Department has
clarified that under  the Scheme of ‘Revision of Pay Scales of University and College Teachers’, Central Government is
to provide financial assistance to the State Governments for the period from 1.1.1996 to 31.3.2000 only to the extent of
80% of the additional expenditure involved in implementation of the Scheme.   An amount of Rs. 1511.80 crore has
already been released to the State Governments so far.  An amount of Rs. 600.00 crore was allocated for 2000-2001 for
disbursement to the State Governments.   This allocation was stepped up to Rs. 1060.00 crore at the RE stage keeping in
view the claims submitted/proposed to be submitted by the State Governments.  Since the claims of all the State
Governments were proposed to be settled in 2000-2001 the BE for 2001-2002 has been kept at Rs. 2.81 crore, as against
Rs. 600.00 crore provided last year.   However, some of the State Governments have not yet submitted their proposals in
the absence of which the RE is proposed to be kept at Rs. 825.00 crore.
2.4       The Committee has been given to understand that during 2001-2002,  vocationalisation of secondary education,
computer education in schools, revision of school curriculum, educational technology, expansion of Navodaya
Vidyalayas, quality upgradation in higher education sector, strengthening of distance mode of education, substantial
increase in the output of technical manpower, creation and augmentation of capacity in the field of information
technology, upgradation of Regional Engineering Colleges into world-class institutions, strengthening of national level
institutions like IITs, IIMs, IISc.  etc.   will be the major areas of priority.  

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/104threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:17]
2.5       The Committee observes that the projected requirement of the Department during Ninth Plan was Rs. 15,589.77
crore.  During all the five years of Ninth Plan, trend of allocation of funds has been below the requirements as projected
by the Department.  The Committee is constrained to observe that during the first four years of Ninth Plan, allocations
have been invariably reduced at the RE stage substantially or marginally and  even this reduced provision continued to
be under utilized except during 1999-2000.  The Committee notes that against the RE allocation of Rs. 1700.00 crore in
2000-2001, expenditure reported upto 16.2.2001, is only Rs. 1179.97 crore.  The Committee is, therefore, of the view
that the Department should make concerted efforts for optimum utilisation of allocated funds in accordance with the
physical and financial targets set for different schemes of both secondary and higher education.
III        NATIONAL COUNCIL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH & TRAINING (NCERT)
3.1       Plan allocation for NCERT in 2000-2001 was Rs.13.00 crore which was reduced to Rs.10.00 crore at the RE
stage and allocation in BE 2001-2002 is Rs.11.20 crore which is still less than last year’s BE allocation. The Department
has clarified that the Plan allocation of NCERT was reduced last year at RE stage from Rs. 13.00 crore to  Rs. 10.00
crore as NCERT had an unspent balance of Rs.2.83 crore as on 1.4.2000. Against the projected demand of Rs. 13.00
crore for 2001-2002, the Planning Division of the Department reduced this to Rs.11.20 crore. 
3.2       The Committee has been informed that the NCERT has completed the review of the 10 year old National
Curriculum Framework and has brought out the National Curriculum Framework during November, 2000 which has
been circulated to all the State Governments/UTs and Boards etc. for further consideration.  It was clarified that a
discussion document on National Curriculum Framework was released in January, 2000 and was sent to all the State
Education Ministers, Chairman of Boards of School Education, Directors of SCERTs, NGOs etc. for their comments
and suggestions.   Regional Seminars were also organized to discuss the draft document in different   States.   The
document was also placed before Governing Body of the NCERT in which all the State Governments. are represented
through their respective Education Ministers.   The Committee was given to understand that about 12-13 State
Education Ministers participated in this meeting.   NCERT is also planning to conduct meetings in different States in
this issue and one meeting has already been held in Tripura.   The Committee desires that a meeting of Central Advisory
Board on Education (CABE) may also be convened by the Department on this issue.   
IV        KENDIRIYA VIDALAYA SANGATHAN (KVS)
4.1       BE allocation for the year 1999-2000 for Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan was Rs.544.81 crore which got
enhanced to Rs.590.59 crore in 2000-2001 Non Plan allocation of Rs.454.81 crore enhanced to Rs.495.59 crore in 2000-
2001  was primarily meant for meeting the expenditure on pay and allowances, retirement benefits and cost of essential
services.  Plan allocation was enhanced to Rs.95.00 crore in 2000-2001 against an allocation  Rs.90.00 crore in 1999-
2000 for maintenance and repairs of school buildings affected by severe cyclone in Orissa. However, the Committee has
been informed that only a small amount of Plan funds i.e.  Rs.4.57 lakhs was required for carrying out special repairs of
school buildings and staff quarters affected by the cyclone in Ganjam District of Orissa on 17.10.1999 which was
sanctioned by KVS in May, 2000.
4.2       The cyclone affected the coastal Districts of Orissa, particularly Ganjam, Balasore, Bhadrak, Cuttack, Puri,
Khurda, Dhenkanal, Kendrapara and other places from 28/10/1999 onwards.  The Committee is, however, perturbed to
note that  only a small amount has been sanctioned for Ganjam District alone and that too only  in May, 2000 i.e after 6-
7 months.  The Committee wonders whether no damage was caused to the KV School Buildings in any of the costal
districts of Orissa due to the cyclone.  In case, there were other school buildings affected by the  cyclone, funds should
have been sanctioned and released for their construction/repairs.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the
number of KVS functioning in  Orissa (district wise) and status of schools damaged by the cyclone in 1999.
4.3       Last year, the Committee was given to understand that construction work was in progress in 79 KV Schools.   
The Committee observes that out of the 79 Kendriya Vidyalayas, construction works have been completed in respect of 
KV, Leh and KV No.1, Itanagar. As per the latest information, buildings plans are under preparation/processing for 73
KVS.  The  Committee expresses its dissatisfaction over the slow progress of construction works of KVs.  The
Committee recommends that there should be proper monitoring of construction works of the KVS so as to complete the
projects in a fixed time frame.

has also been  informed that out of the 440 Vidyalayas sanctioned so far, construction of buildings has been sanctioned
for 380 Vidyalayas.  Out of this, 286 Vidyalayas are functioning in their own buildings with the construction of
buildings of 158 Vidyalayas having been completed and buildings of 128 Vidyalayas are in advanced stage of

sanctioned and the remaining 36 JNVs are expected to be sanctioned during 2001-2002, i.e. the last year of the Ninth

5.4       The Committee is constrained to observe that a number of states have not transferred the land for construction of
JNVs, as assured by them, with the result construction of as many as 60 schools could not be undertaken.  The

 VI       VOCATIONALISATION OF EDUCATION

created 19,455 sections in 6728 schools, thus providing diversion of over 10 lakh students at +2 level.  So far Rs. 645.98
crore have been released.  Most of the states have shown progress in implementation of the scheme.

per the norms following which the proposal will be put up to SFC/EFC for necessary approval after obtaining the
estimates from the CPWD.  The Committee is of the view that all procedural formalities should be expedited and funds
allocated so that construction of the building of PSSCIVE, Bhopal is started at the earliest.
VII       COMPUTER EDUCATION IN SCHOOLS, [ERSTWHILE SCHEME OF COMPUTER LITERACY AND
STUDIES IN SCHOOLS (CLASS)]
7.1       A pilot project on Computer Literacy and Studies in Schools (CLASS) was initiated in 1984-85.  The project
continued upto 1992-93 on adhoc basis.  The implementation of CLASS project was then reviewed by C&AG.  The
C+AG report identified multiplicity of agencies, diffused responsibility and inadequate monitoring etc.  Accordingly, a
modified scheme was prepared and introduced from 1993-94 which continued to be implemented as a Centrally
Sponsored Scheme upto 1999.  2371 schools were covered under the modified scheme during Eighth Plan.  However, in
the meanwhile, on the advice of the Ministry of Finance, it was decided that the scheme be phased out and only
maintenance funds were to be released to States/UTs.  All the State Govts/UT Administrations were, accordingly, 
informed about the discontinuance of the scheme  from 1.4.99.      
7.2       The latest position is that a revised scheme in place of erstwhile Computer Literacy and Studies in School
(CLASS) Scheme is in an advanced stage of formulation and is expected to be operationalised during 2001-2002.  
When asked about the necessity of revising the scheme, the Department has stated that the very nature of the erstwhile
scheme was “Supply driven”  and there was little involvement of teachers and students with the scheme.  Therefore, the
progress of the scheme remained slow.   In the new scheme, attempts have been made to correct these shortcomings. 
The Committee has been further informed that the proposed scheme would not be a `stand alone’ scheme and would aim
at  capturing the developments which are taking place  in the field of IT Education in various States.   The revised

scheme would be posited within the overall environment in each State in which diverse measures for imparting IT
education are being taken at various levels and seek to catalyse convergence.
7.3       The Committee observes that the BE 2000-2001 for `Computer Education in Schools’ under Plan  was Rs. 30.00
crore which got reduced to a meagre Rs. 5.00 crore at RE stage.  An enhanced allocation of Rs. 84.50 crore has been
proposed for 2001-2002.  On a specific query about the reason for this fluctuation,  the Department has clarified that the
allocation of Rs. 30.00 crore was kept for meeting the requirements of the revised scheme of Computer Literacy and
Studies in Schools.   However as the revised scheme could not be operationalized during 2000-2001,   a provision of Rs.
5.00 crore was kept to meet the pending maintenance grants incurred   by States on the scheme.   The increased
allocation of Rs. 84.50 crore has been proposed  for 2001-2002 as the revised scheme is in an advanced stage of
formulation and is expected to be operationalised during 2001-2002.
7.4       Element of uncertainly hanging over the CLASS Scheme has been engaging the attention of the Committee for
the last two-three years.  The Committee is constrained to observe that only maintenance funds are being allocated
under this Scheme almost from the beginning of Ninth Plan.  Even these funds are being drastically reduced at the RE
stage.  What is more discouraging is that the reduced funds also remained under-utilized as indicated below :—

VIII      INTEGRATED EDUCATION FOR DISABLED CHILDREN (IEDC)
8.1       The Scheme of Integrated Education for Disabled Children (IEDC) is presently being implemented in 27 states
and 5 UTs with over 22,000 schools benefiting  more than 95,000 disabled children.  The scheme is being implemented
by State Govts. as well as NGOs.
8.2       The Committee has been informed that the financial outlay for IEDC scheme in the Ninth Plan period is Rs.100
crore.  During the first four years of the Ninth Plan, about Rs.46.69 crore have been spent in the implementation of the
scheme.  The BE allocation for 2001-2002 has been kept at Rs.21.40 cores.  The Committee is  constrained to observe 
that the allocation for the Ninth Plan for the Scheme will not be fully utilized, giving an impression that the
implementations of the Scheme is not satisfactory.
8.3       As per the details of students/schools covered under the scheme upto 1999-2000, Goa, Meghalaya, Sikkim, J &K
and UT  of Chandigarh do not seem to be participating at all.  In contrast, in States like Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat,
Orissa, Tamil Nadu and Haryana, both State Govts. and NGOs are actively involved.  The Committee observes that in
West Bengal whereas it seems every year new school is being taken up by State Govt. for implementation of the
scheme, 169 students in 81 schools have been covered upto 1999-2000 by 2 NGOs.  Case of UP seems to be even
worse.  Grants released for 32 schools (figures of students not available) are lying unspent for long.  In contrast, 6
NGOs are managing 667 students in 265 schools.  The Scheme of Integrated Education for the Disabled Children
(IEDC) launched in 1974 has undergone two revisions, so far.  The Committee is, however, perturbed to note that the
scheme is not being implemented properly due to non-availability of infrastructure/financial assistance/specially
qualified teachers with States/UTs.
8.4       Last year, the Committee  was informed that NCERT had been requested to conduct an impact study with a view
of ascertaining the impact of the IEDC Scheme.  It seems that not much progress has been made by NCERT in this
matter.  The Committee is of the view that this study should be expedited by NCERT.  The Committee would also like
to emphasise that there is an urgent need for having an effective monitoring mechanism for this scheme.

22.1     The Committee over the years has observed that a higher provision is generally made in the BE which is

be ensured that no scheme is launched and budget provisions made therefor during the period without proper scrutiny.

reduction in the allocation of funds is not resorted to at the RE stage for two-three years on a continuous basis.

The Committee observes that the projected requirement of the Department during Ninth Plan was Rs. 15,589.77 crore. 
During all the five years of Ninth Plan, trend of allocation of funds has been below the requirements as projected by the
Department.  The Committee is constrained to observe that during the first four years of Ninth Plan, allocations have
been invariably reduced at the RE stage substantially or marginally and  even this reduced provision continued to be
under utilized except during 1999-2000.  The Committee notes that against the RE allocation of Rs. 1700.00 crore in
2000-2001, expenditure reported upto 16.2.2001, is only Rs. 1179.97 crore.  The Committee is, therefore, of the view
that the Department should make concerted efforts for optimum utilisation of allocated funds in accordance with the
physical and financial targets set for different schemes of both secondary and higher education. (Para 2.5)

States.   The document was also placed before Governing Body of the NCERT in which all the State Governments. are
represented through their respective Education Ministers.   The Committee was given to understand that about 12-13
State Education Ministers participated in this meeting.   NCERT is also planning to conduct meetings in different States
in this issue and one meeting has already been held in Tripura.   The Committee desires that a meeting of Central
Advisory Board on Education (CABE) may also be convened by the Department on this issue.    (Para 3.2)

I.             Methods of computing drop out rate
Observation of the Committee
            
The Committee during its visit had held discussions with many NGOs  and experts working in the field of education and
felt that there is a lot of ambiguity about the method of commuting the drop out rate.   In view thereof the Committee wishes
here to redefine the definition of the popular methods which are used for computing drop out rates.   The three methods for
determining drop-out rates are as under:-
a)                  Method based on grade-to-grade progression rates.
b)                  Method based on ratio of grade V enrolment to grade I enrolment of 5 years before; and
c)                  Methods based on individual students data on their year to year progress in schools.
The Committee recommends that the three above-mentioned methods may be used as parameters to locate dropouts for
which a Retention Register should be maintained.
Comments of the Department
Responses have been received from ten States and UTs (Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Andaman and Nicobar, Daman,
Tripura, Pondicherry, Goa, Maharashtra, Haryana, Arunachal Pradesh and Gujarat).   All have agreed with the recommendation
of the Parliamentary Standing Committee that the three methods mentioned should be used as parameters to locate drop out for
which a Retention Register should be maintained.
            On a specific query about the response of the remaining States, the Department informed that the issue was inter-alia
discussed in the meeting of the State Education Secretaries at New Delhi on August 28-29, 2000.    Most of the Secretaries were
in agreement with the recommendation of the Committee and felt that there was need to review the existing procedures in this
regard.   Tamil Nadu has completed a sample study based on retrospective cohort method.  Some of the States like Andhra
Pradesh, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, and Haryana have also initiated  such studies.
II.            Enrolment Ratio
Observation of the Committee
2.1        The Committee is of the opinion that enrolment ratio and drop-out rates are co-related.   Accurate drop out rate can be
arrived at only on the basis of actual enrolment ratio.  However, the  Committee understands that this is not the position in most
of the States.   At present, what is happening is that Headmaster of a primary school simply shows all school going  children in
the village as enrolled in his school in class I.    No consideration is being given to the percentage of children actually attending
the school on a regular basis.   Besides that, problem of double enrolment was often found in evidence by the Committee during
its State visits.   The Committee feels that accurate enrolment figures can be easily arrived at by involving the Village Education
Committees and local youth in this task.   The Committee also recommends that the admission age of the child in Class I should
be strictly adhered to in order to avoid the instances of fictitious enrolment.
Comments of the Department
            All States and UTs. whose response has been received endorse the recommendation of the Parliamentary Standing
Committee.   Village Education Committees are being involved to arrive at accurate enrolment figures.   In DPEP, involvement
of VECs for microplanning, which includes  household surveys, has been stressed.   Efforts will be made to incorporate the
valuable recommendations of the Committee while implementing the proposed Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan – an effort for UEE in a
mission mode following a holistic and convergent approach.
            The Department has further informed that the recommendation of the Committee has been incorporated in the draft

guidelines of the proposed scheme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan  which provides for eight years of elementary schooling for all

IV.            Opening of more Primary and Upper Primary Schools
Observation of the Committee
4.3        The Committee recommends that the norms for opening new schools in remote, hilly and desert areas should be relaxed
and the Village Education Committees (VECs) should be empowered to make survey of the existing situation, identification of
non-schooling areas and preparation of plan for facilitating the State Governments to open good quality non-formal education
centres.   Keeping in view the growth rate of population, the Central Government should also make plans for creating extra
upper primary schooling facilities equal to the primary schools in the country.
Comments of the Department
            Under the revised NFE scheme named Alternative and Innovative Education, provision to establish Education Guarantee
Centres in unserved habitations has been made. Under the proposed Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan upgradation of primary to upper
primary schools is an item of financing.  Vertical expansion of DPEP to cover upper primary is also under consideration.
            The Department further clarified that the  revised EGS & AIE scheme provides for setting up of alternative schools
commonly named as EGS(Education Guarantee Scheme)  schools in all habitations that do not have primary schools within a
radius of one Km.  This would specially benefit hilly, desert and remote areas.   It was expected that about 50,000 EGS schools
may be supported under the scheme during 2000-2001, if proposals were received from the States.  It also provides for running
of alternative schools for upper primary stage for which per pupil cost has been enhanced from Rs.580/- to Rs.1200/- per
annum.  The other intervention for older children in the age group 11-14  will also be possible in the form of residential camp,
remedial teaching and special camps for adolescent  girls.
            Under this scheme, the community and Village Education Committees(VECs of Panchayats) have been given a central
role in running of the schools including conduct of micro-planning, selection of the volunteer teachers, payment of honorarium
and overall management of the school/centre.  The scheme also provides for setting up of upper primary level centres.
            The proposed scheme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan envisages :
-
                Upgradation and provision of upper primary schools/sections as per requirement based on number of children
completing the primary stage up to a ceiling of one upper primary school/section for every two primary schools.
-                Provision of one teacher and one classroom for every class and a room for the headmaster in every upper primary
school.
 
If also provides for running of alternative schools for upper primary stage for which per pupil cost has been enhanced
from Rs.580/- to Rs.1200/- per child per annum.  The other intervention for older children in the age group 11-14  will also be
possible in the form of residential camp, remedial teaching and special camps for adolescent  girls.
Observation of the Committee
4.4        The Committee hopes that a funding pattern under JRY worked out by the Department of Education in consultation with
the Ministry of Rural Development would accelerate the pace of construction of schools buildings.
Comments of the Department
From the savings under the JGSY, funds for primary school buildings can be provided on a 75-25  sharing with States.
V.       Joyful Learning
Observation of the Committee
5.1             The Committee during its visits has seen that the present system of imparting education to the children is very
traditional and rigid and is not based on scientific pattern.   The Committee is of the view that Text-books should be colourful
and attractive from the children point of view and oral joyful teaching learning mechanism should be introduced at least upto
IIIrd standard as the Committee observed that the maximum rate of drop out is from Class I to Class III.

5.2        The Committee feels that schools can be made an attractive place and learning a joyful experience, if teaching is made
child centred and activity oriented as has been done in the `Anandapath’  schooling system adopted by the Government of West
Bengal and also by production of colourful and attractive textbooks and low cost teaching aids.   The creation of these items
would automatically result in improving the retention rate.
Comments of the Department
            The task of making learning joyful has been undertaken in many states, especially under DPEP.   New textbooks and
workbooks, teacher training modules, etc.   have been developed to make learning joyful.
            Government of Gujarat has informed that already more than 30,000 Balmitra Vargas have been established that provide
activity based learning to students of class I.   New textbooks prepared under Lok Jumbish Project in Rajasthan and under DPEP
in Kerala, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradsh and Maharashtra have focused on
activity-based and child-centred learning.
VI.            Motivation of Teacher
Observation of the Committee
6.1        The Committee feels that lack of motivation on the part of a section of teachers is indirectly responsible for dismal
retention rate of students in the schools.   Dedicated teachers are required for making the stay of a child in school a joyful
experience.   However, at present this is not very much visible  primarily in the Government set-up of schools.   The Committee
is of the considered view that inculcation of motivation can be successfully attempted by making it an essential component of
teachers’ training programme. 
Comments of the Department
NCERT has noted the Committee’s useful suggestion of making motivational training a part of teacher training
modules.   NCERT is providing academic support to SCERTS to organize teachers training programme on an ongoing basis.
Observation of the Committee
6.2        The Committee finds that almost all the states have the required strength of teachers.   But mere filling up of the existing
vacancies of teachers is not the end, but it is just the beginning.   The Committee feels that motivated, dedicated and fully
trained teachers are the need of the hour.   The Committee finds that all the State Councils of Educational Research and Training
(SCERTs) are not fully equipped to impart adequate training to the teachers.   Even many of the SCERTs  personnel require
training by master trainers.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that NCERT should launch a pilot programme in close
collaboration with the SCERTs  for the training of teachers.   This becomes all the more necessary as studies have pointed out
that the utilisation of teaching learning material has not been very satisfactory because of lack of training of teachers.   The
Committee  is of the considered view that if teachers are imparted training on how to use available equipment effectively in a
classroom teaching situation, it is bound to have a positive impact on improvement in quality of teaching.
Comments of the Department
NCERT has informed that SCERTs and DIETs are being provided academic support by NCERT to equip them to
organize training programmes on a continuing basis.
Observation of the Committee
6.3        The Committee is in full agreement with the findings of  evaluation of the `Operation Blackboard’ that there is a need
to:-
(i)                 streamline the purchase procedure with inbuilt quality controls;
(ii)                Provide for greater involvement of teachers in selection of teaching aids;
(iii)              Develop better linkage between teaching aids and curriculum requirements; and
(iv)              Motivate teachers to improve teachers aids from inexpensive locally available materials.
Comments of the Department
            States are making efforts in this direction.   The Central Government has been emphasizing the need for decentralized
procurement of teaching aids with full involvement of teachers and representatives of PRIs.   In DPEP, a provision has been
made for  Rs. 500/- grant for the teacher to prepare/purchase teaching learning materials of his/her choice.   The teaching
learning material grants are contextually situated and developed as per the curriculum requirement in DPEP.

Observation  of the Committee
During the visit of the Committee to certain States, it observed that there were some districts maintaining very high
drop-out rates and among the low level drop-out districts, there were some blocks having high drop-out rate.  There are also
some villages with high drop-out rate in such districts.  Thus, the drop-out problem is prevalent throughout the country.  The

in the age group of 6-14 years.   The Committee feels that this kind of school mapping exercise should be undertaken in all the

Comments of the Department
            The proposed Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan provides for school mapping and micro planning with the involvement of the local
