X.                 Setting up Junior Technical/Vocational Education Institute
Observation  of the Committee
10.1            The Committee was given to understand during the field visits by the State Governments that the drop-out rates are
very high in classes VII or VIII.   The primary reasons for this situation is that there is a general feeling among parents/students
that no purpose would be served by continuing studies after class VIII.   To check this high drop-out rate, the Committee is of
the opinion that some technical/vocational education institutes should be set up for imparting two years’ certificate courses in
the field of craft, carpentry, mechanical, food processing and poultry farms etc. after VIIIth Standard.   The Committee feels that
setting up of such institutes would not only give a pragmatic approach towards the educational system but it will also help in
earning their livelihood and for inculcating an attitude towards vocationalisation.
10.2
         The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Education and the Planning Commission should initiate
action for setting up of technical/vocational education institutes parallel to the secondary stage in some selected districts on an
experimental basis and make budgetary provision accordingly in the 9th Plan.
Comments of the Department
           The scheme of vocational education is under review at present.   The valuable suggestions of the Parliamentary Standing
Committee would be taken note of while formulating the revised scheme.
XII.     Mid-Day Meal Scheme
Observation of the Committee
12.1            The Mid-Day Meal Scheme was launched by the Central Govt. on 15 th August, 1995 to give a boost to the
universalisation of Primary Education by impacting upon enrolment, attendance, retention and the nutrition needs of children in
Primary Classes.   The Committee has noticed that cooked meal is not being served in all the States and instead 3 kg. Wheat/rice
is being distributed to the children in many states without adhering to the stipulated condition of 80% attendance in a month.  
The Committee was apprised that the attendance rate on the day of distribution only remained very high.
12.2
            The Committee feels that to have a direct impact of the Mid-day Meal Scheme on the retention side, to check the
problem of absenteeism and drop-out and also to provide nutrition to the school going children instead of distributing 3 kg.
Wheat/rice, cooked meal should be served.
12.3            During the study visits, the Committee also noticed that pilferages are taking place and the distribution system of
foodgrains has also not been developed systematically due to which untimely and short supply are the frequent phenomena
which could be judged from the fact that in some of the States/UTs.  like Rajasthan, West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar
Islands, foodgrains have not been distributed to the tragetted group even once in the academic session of 1996-97.
12.4            The  Committee makes the following recommendations to correct the above- mentioned situation:-
(1)          Cooked meal should be served;
(2)          Strict monitoring system delegating the power to Village Level Education Committee or PTA should be evolved;
(3)          Co-ordination between the Civil Supply and Education Department of State Governments needs to be
strengthened;
(4)         Local youth may be involved for the preparation of the cooked food; and

(5)         Mid-day meal should be provided through a separate mechanism without disturbing the normal academic
work of Teachers.
(6)         The Noon Meal Programme of Tamil Nadu Government may be adopted as a model for implementing
Mid-Day Meal Scheme.
Comments of the Department
            It was expected that all States would switch over to the serving of hot cooked meals within a period of two years of
commencement of the scheme i.e., by 1997-98.   However, most states/UTs have, so far, opted for distribution of foodgrains
under the programme.   Five States namely, Gujarat, Kerala, Orissa, Tamil Nadu and Madhya Pradesh (limited to 174 tribal
blocks) and Union Territory of Pondicherry are providing cooked meals.   Government of UT of Delhi has been supplying
processed food in urban slums.   Haryana  and J&K which started with a cooked meal reverted to distribution of foodgrains as
did Madhya Pradesh for the non-tribal blocks in the States.
            The State Govts. are expected  to bear the cost of conversion of foodgrains into a cooked meal though support for
construction of a kitchen shed and wages for a cook are available from funds from programmes of the Ministry of Rural Areas
and Employment.   The main reason for not switching over to hot cooked meals and instead providing foodgrains alone is the
paucity of funds.   It has been estimated that in the Ninth Plan alone, Rs. 18,000 crore would be required to convert foodgrains
to hot cooked meals, as against a requirement of Rs. 12,615 crores for the supply of foodgrains alone.
            The guidelines of NP-NSPE provided that the impelenting agencies of the programme will be Local Bodies/Authorities
such as panchayats and Nagar Palikas.  The Local Bodies will have flexibility to organize and to decide the type of food to be
provided and are also expected to develop institutional arrangements for providing cooked/pre-cooked food in association with
the Village Education Committees (VECs), School Parent Teacher Associations, women/DWACRA groups and other
organizations.
            At the State level a nodal Department is responsible for implementation of the programme.   In case, the designated
department is other than the Education Department, necessary linkages are established between the designated department and
the Primary Education Department.   Towards this end, it has been suggested to the State Governments that an institutional
mechanism of a Committee under the Chairmanship of the Chief Secretary/Additional Chief Secretary/Development
Commissioner be constituted to oversee the implementation of the programme.   The Committee should include the Secretaries
and Heads of Department of all the concerned Departments and is expected to ensure the convergence of primary education,
primary health care, early childhood care and education, nutrition and other related services.
            In order to provide logistic support, employment  schemes have already been linked with this programme.   As stated in
the guidelines, expenditure on remuneration of cooks/helpers and construction of sheds under this programme is to be met out of
the JRY/NRY funds of the Ministry of Rural Areas and Employment and Ministry of Urban Areas and Employment  for rural
and urban areas respectively.
            The Department has requested State Chief Secretaries and Education Departments to ensure that teachers are not
involved in the distribution of foodgrains to the extent possible and that adequate support be provided to them at school level
through local bodies and community based organizations such as Mahila Mandals, Women Groups and PTAs.
            Under NP-NSPE the implementing agencies/Local Bodies/authorities such as Panchayats and Nagarpalikas have the
flexibility to organize, to decide the type of food to be provided subject to the food being wholesome and having a calorific
value equivalent to 100 gms of wheat/rice per student per day.  Eating habits being different from state to state, it may not be
feasible to adopt a uniform model for all parts of the country.   The Giri Committee   on Mid-Day Meals had considered various
models including the Tamil Nadu model, before making recommendations for introduction of NP-NSPE on the existing
pattern.   Nevertheless, State Governments have the flexibility to adopt the scheme to their requirements.
            The recommendations of the Committee have been communicated to the States.   Steps have also been taken by Govt. of
India to ensure closer monitoring of the implementation of the programme.
            A study of the programme by an independent Consultant, Operations Research Group, New Delhi in ten states found that
in Assam, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal there has been a boost to enrolment whereas in Gujarat, Haryana,
Jammu and Kashmir, Karnataka, Orissa and Rajasthan the programme has made a positive impact on attendance and retention.

XIV.            Distribution of Free Text Books
Observation of the Committee
14.1      In most of the States, free text books are being distributed  amongst the children upto Class V but the Committee during

XV.      Girls Education/Women’s Development
Observation of the Committee
15.2      The Committee recommends for giving suitable incentives to girl child, like providing free uniform, free
teaching/learning materials and construction of toilet and providing drinking water facilities particularly in the girls school/co-
education schools.   The Committee also recommends that a Special Management Structure should be set up wherein women
should be placed in the key position and at the micro level women’s groups should be engaged for the development of the girl
child.
15.3      As women have traditionally played a subordinate role in society,  so they have been conditioned into thinking of
themselves as inferior to men, to be tolerated only if they toil, fetch, carry and procreate.   Financial burden is only hurdle in the
education of boys but it becomes an insurmountable barrier when the question of education of girls arises.   Sending her to
school would also mean an additional loss of income because the mother will have to stay away from work to look after the
younger ones and to do the household chores.   But education can be an enduring and strong factor in women’s empowerment.
15.4      The Committee feels that unless a systematic effort is made to improve women’s access to education it will not be
possible to achieve the objective of education for all by the year 2000.   Experience has shown that the rural women have  not
kept pace with the ‘Sathin’s’ progress.   It is now a recognized fact that instead of focussing on just one woman, `Sathin’ village
level activity should be central around a Group of women.   The Committee is of the view that this collective, the Samooh, after
adequate orientation and training would enable the village women to take an interest and play an effective role in community
activities especially related to Education.
Comments of the Department
            Most of the States are providing free education for girls upto upper primary/secondary level with provision of free text
books and uniforms for SC/ST girls.            In pursuance of the National Agenda for Governance (NAG) 1998, this Ministry has
proposed launching a scheme called “National Strategy for ensuring greater participation of women in educational field.”
The scheme envisages developing multiple facilities to provide access and other incentives for provision of girls education and
for their retention as also creation of assets in favour  of rural poor, particularly the SCs/STs and educationally backward
minorities.   These include girls’ hostels, book banks, Navodaya Schools and remedial coaching classes etc.
            This Ministry had also launched in 1989, a programme called ‘Mahila Samakhya’ (Education for Women’s Equality). 
The basic objective of Mahila Samakhya  (M.S.) is to promote empowerment of women through education.  The programme
seeks to bring about a change in women’s perception about themselves  and that of society in regard to women’s traditional
role.  The M.S.’s interventions in adult education, literacy, NFE and ECCE have generated  a positive demand among rural
women for education.  Mahila Samakhya has made special efforts for girls education by creating an enabling environment
through Mahila Sangha and by holding Bal Shiksha Mela and providing training input to teachers.

 XVII.   Community Involvement

XV.      Girls Education/Women’s Development
Observation of the Committee
15.1      The survey carried out in the field of education reveals that education has been an intervention for women’s equality
and the time has now come that Government should make its utmost efforts so that the existing gap between the girls and boys
is bridged.   Unfortunately, in India, girls’ educational deprivation is the most glaring manifestation of India’s educational
backwardness and the education indicators are very adverse in classes 1 to V and 1 to VIII.   The All India drop out rate for
1995-96 amongst the girls in classes 1 to V is 38.35% and in classes 1 to VIII it is 52.77% which is very high.   The main reason
for this large number of drop-out rate is that the girls are engaged in house hold work such as fuel and fodder collection,
fetching of water and care of siblings etc.

monitoring the Enrolment, Retention and Progression Registers should be assigned to the Village Level Education Committee
Comments of the Department
3.3        All States/UTs which have responded agree with the recommendation of the Parliamentary Standing Committee.  In
DPEP, an Educational  Management Information System (EMIS) to computerize educational data has been developed.   The
need for improved data quality and cross checking has been stressed.
On a specific query by the Committee about steps taken by the Department for improving the quality of data, the
Department informed that a Committee on Educational Statistics has been constituted.   Provision for establishment of
Education MIS is part of the proposals for preparatory  activities under the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan.   Besides that, 219 DPEP
districts have established effective EMIS and the data is regularly analysed.   For example, in Tamil Nadu, previous year’s data
is being maintained school wise by the Block Education Officer and the data contained in the Data Capture  Format (DCF) is
duly certified/authenticated by him.   Similarly, in Orissa, Karnataka and Kerala, the data is crosschecked by Cluster Resource
Centre Co-ordinator  (RCC).
Recommendation of the Committee
            The Committee takes note of the various measures initiated by the Department for improving the quality  of data with
respect to maintenance of Enrolment, Progression and Retention Registers for monitoring the drop-out rate in primary and upper
primary schools.   The Committee hopes that all these measures would result in increased enrolment and retention of students.   
The Committee, however, is of the view that alongwith computerized data, field level visits both at regular intervals and without
prior notice should also continue.   The Committee notes that its recommendation regarding maintenance  of Enrolment,
Retention and Progress Registers by the Village Education Committees has been endorsed by all the States and UTs.  and hopes
that the same will be implemented at the earliest.
IV.            Opening of More Primary and Upper Primary Schools
Observation of the Committee
4.1        The scheme of `Operation Blackboard’ was launched in 1987 with the objective to bring about both qualitative and
quantitative improvement in primary education.   Central Government has extended financial assistance to the extent of Rs.
1551.68 crores from  1987-88 till 31st March, 1995.   However, till 31st March, 1995 only 81%  of the total Central funds i.e. Rs.
1253.09 crores  could be utilized by the States.
Comments of the Department
            Some States have reported higher utilization.   Others have mentioned that funds released in the last financial year would
be utilized  shortly.
            When specifically asked to clarify  the present position of utilisation of funds by the States,  the Department informed
that under the scheme of Operation Blackboard (OB), Central Govt. has extended financial assistance to the extent of Rs.
2617.26 crores from 1987-88 till 31 st March, 2000.  The utilization percentage of the funds sanctioned for teaching learning
equipment and salaries of teachers appointed under OB is 86.29%.   Thus, there is an improvement of over 5%.  Most of the
unutilized funds are for procurement of TLE which involves various procedures such as identifying material, advertising,

107th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/107threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:18]
inviting and processing tender, executing agreement etc.  In order to further accelerate the pace of utilization, the State Govts.
have been asked to decentralize procurement of TLE.
Recommendation of the Committee
            The Committee expresses its grave concern over non-utilisation of around 14% of the financial assistance under
Operation Blackboard given to the States by the Centre.  Basic infrastructure in most of the schools in the country is still lacking
and there is  greater demand for quantitative as well as qualitative improvements in elementary education.   In this context, a
mere request to States to decentralize procurement of Teaching Learning Equipment may not be enough.   The Committee,
therefore,  recommends that Ministry may thoroughly look into this issue and take suitable remedial measures for full and
proper utilisation of Central funds.
Observation of the Committee
4.2        Even after a decade of the launching of Operation Blackboard, the Committee finds that so far as basic infrastructure is
concerned, it cannot be said that all the primary schools all over the country are fully provided for.   The Schools visited by the
Committee during its study tours were selected in advance by the State Governments.   So, they cannot be said to be true
reflection of the physical state of primary schools.  Even then the Committee is constrained to state that these  pre-arranged
schools were also lacking in basic facilities.   No doubt, by and large, school buildings were there and in some cases extensions
were also being carried on.   But these were insufficient to the needs of school-going children.   Drinking water and toilet
facilities were also inadequate.   In some of the schools, which the Committee visited, the students were being made to sit on
bare floor.   The Committee also observed that in majority of primary schools, two or three classes were being held in one room
under the supervision of only one teacher.   The Committee feels that this state of affairs is responsible, to some extent, for  non-
retention of children in schools.  Urgent steps, therefore, need to be taken for creating facilities so that every class has its
separate room.   The Committee during its visits noticed that due to non-availability of infrastructure and lack of schools, very
large number of children, perhaps 20%, do not have access to school.   The problem is particularly more grave at the upper
primary stage from class VI to VIII specially in the case of girls.   On ascertaining the reasons for not opening new schools, the
Committee was informed that the rigid norms for opening new schools  and increase in the population of the State are the main
barrier, resulting in more out-of- school children.
Comments of the Department
            While there has been progress in provision of school facilities under Operation Blackboard, the assessment of the
Parliamentary Standing Committee is very correct that much more needs to be done in order to provide basic infrastructure for
all children.   The States and UTs  have indicated the efforts being made by them.   Govt. of Maharashtra has pointed out that
inspite of maximum allocation of funds for construction of classrooms, there is still a need to construct about 52000 classrooms
in that State.   It has suggested that Govt. of India sanction 100% grants for construction of school rooms under JRY under the
revised guidelines for Jawahar Gram Samriddhi Yojana.   From the saving under the Yojana, school buildings can be
constructed on 75-25 sharing (Centre-State).  Besides funds under Ministry of Rural Development, construction of classrooms is
also taking place under the District Primary Education Programme and Lok Jumbish Project.  Govt. of Gujarat has liberalized
the norms for upgrading lower primary schools to upper primary schools and 4200 lower  primary schools are being upgraded
this year.   Andman and Nicobar has no rigid norm for opening schools.  The statement showing the funds released since
inception uptill 1999-2000 under Jawahar Rozgar Yojana/ Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana, for construction of school buildings
under Operation Black Board (OB) is at Annexure-I.   As per the information available, 1,82,381 classrooms have been
constructed under the scheme by 31.3.2000.
            It was clarified by the Department that funds are released for construction of school buildings under Operation
Blackboard (OB) out of saving, if any, from Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana/JRY.   Rural Development Department of the State
Govt. co-ordinates with the State Education Department for submission of proposal under OB.   The funding pattern under the
scheme is 75:25 between the Centre and the State Rural Development Departments.   The Funds under the scheme are to be
released directly to the DRDAS/ZPs.
Recommendations of the Committee
The Committee notes that an amount of Rs. 35,366.53 lakhs has been released to various States during the period 1990-
2000 and 1,82,381 classrooms have been constructed upto 31.3.2000.  States like Orissa, A.P., Assam, Karnataka and  M.P.
have been the major beneficiaries.   However, no release could be made under GSY/JRY to Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, U.P. West
Bengal after 1992-93, in case of Goa only once in 1992-93, only in 1991-92 in respect of Meghalaya and in respect of
Pondicherry  only in 1990-91.   The Committee also notes that Bihar could not take the benefit of the scheme as apparently there
was no saving under JRY/GSY.   The Committee feels that some alternative source of funding has to be provided keeping in
view the financial position of the States.

Observation of the Committee
6.4        The Committee is of the considered view that the working environment and workload of teachers,  particularly those
working in rural primary schools, are far from satisfactory and contribute, to a large extent, to lack of motivation on their part.   
Following factors can be cited as responsible for this situation:-
(a)            Schools without adequate buildings and devoid of essential facilities;
(b)            Lack of teaching aids and libraries;
(c)            Heavy curriculum and workload, particularly for rural primary teachers;
(d)
               Multi grade teaching responsibilities without adequate supervisory support;
(e)            Commuting from long distances;
(f)            Lack of proper housing facilities;
(g)                Non-instructuctional and administrative duties such as supervising elections, participating in census operations,
conducting family planning activities etc., producing adverse impact on the main task of teaching.
Comments of the Department
            The States are in agreement with the findings of the Committee.   They are making all efforts to improve the motivation
of teachers.   Motivational training is also imparted to teachers in DPEP in some States.   In addition, through the 24% allocation
of funds for civil works in DPEP, provision of school infrastructure has considerably improved.
Observation of the Committee
6.5        The Committee feels that State Governments should initiate immediate action so as to bring about overall improvement
in the working conditions of teachers.
Comments of the Department
            States are making efforts in this direction.   The Central Government has also issued instructions to states regarding
allowing teachers to carry out their primary task.   Govt. of Gujarat has issued instructions to review non-teaching load of
primary school teachers.
Recommendation of  the Committee
            The Committee has been informed that State Governments are making all efforts to improve the motivation of teachers
and the Central Government has also issued necessary instructions to the State Governments in this regard.   The Committee is
not able to understand as to how the State Governments are going to improve the motivation of teachers and also lessen their
(Teachers’) extra workload to enable them to concentrate on their primary duty of teaching.    It has also been stated that
motivational training is imparted to teachers in DPEP in some States.  The Committee does not feel convinced with this as it is
aware that coverage of DPEP is still very less as a large part of the country still  remains uncovered.   The Committee is
therefore, of the view that the Department needs to address this issue with all seriousness as motivation of teachers is very
important. 
VII.           Change in Examination System
Observation of the Committee
7.1      The Committee finds that in many States students even in primary classes are promoted to the next class only on the
result of the annual examination.   This indirectly acts as a demotivating factor so far as retention of children in schools is
concerned.  There are  a couple of States viz.   Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal where there is no examination system upto the
level of Classes V and VI.   Students are being promoted only on the basis of attendance.
7.2      The Committee, however, recommends that annual examination system as the criteria for promotion to the next class
should continue.
Comments of the Department
           Many states hold annual examination, though promotion to the next class does not necessarily depend on it.   Promotion
is both on the basis of attendance and examination. Regarding annual examination for promoting students to the higher class 
and on the policy of detention, different States follow different criteria and policy. 
Recommendation of the Committee
            The Committee has been informed that different States follow different criteria for promotion to higher class and
detention of the students.   The  Committee feels that it would be better if a uniform policy of promotion and detention is
followed by all the States, taking into consideration all related aspects.   The Committee hopes that the Department would take

initiative in this regard.
IX       Non-Formal Education Programme/Prehar Pathshala as a Backup Method
Observation of the Committee
9.1      Out of school children are being taken care of under the Non-Formal Education Scheme since 1979.   Almost all the
States are running NFE centres.   NGOs are also contributing a lot in this field.   However, even after two decades, the NFE
scheme could not achieve the desired target to bring back the non-formal students to the mainstream education.   There are a
varied number of factors responsible for it.    Poor infrastructure, lack of motivated and trained instructors, very low
honorarium for instructor, lack of community participation, no linkage between Formal and Non-Formal System of education,
NFE being treated as second grade education can be cited as the major reasons for NFE Scheme’s failure.
9.2      The Committee is of the considered view that revamping of entire NFE Scheme with special emphasis on the following
points is urgently required:-
a)
         Creation of Basic facilities at NFE Centres.
b)         Increase in honorarium for instructors.
c)         Involvement of community and  PRIs.
d)         Training of Instructors.
e)         Mechanism for effective supervision and monitoring of NFE Scheme.
Comments of the Department
            The revised scheme of NFE called Alternative and Innovative Education, is in the process of approval.   It has taken into
account the issues suggested by the Parliamentary Standing Committee.   The new scheme is based on different existing,
successful, replicable NFE models in the country.
            Under the revised scheme,
(i)         NFE and the formal system are to be dovetailed into one at the district level where a detailed school mapping
exercise will be undertaken to locate precisely the un served habitations and educationally less privileged areas.
(ii)        Both the community and the PRIs will be actively involved in sharing responsibilities.   They will create the
demand, identify teachers where necessary and provide learning space where required;
(iii)       Honoraria for instructors have been increased five fold.  All costing patterns have been made more realistic;
(iv)       Adequate training and supervision are built in.  The states are free to choose from a set of options.   Non-
academic monitoring and supervision can even be given to the PRIs (as has been done with the Education
Guarantee Scheme in Madhya Pradesh).  Regular training will be organized through the CRCs, BRCs and
DIETs.
             The Department was requested to clarify as to whether NFE under the revised scheme of Alternative and Innovative
Education will be able to provide recognition to non-formal education at  par with the formal education.  The Department
informed that the revised scheme aimed to provide education of a quality comparable /equivalent to the formal schools.   Several
inputs have been included in the scheme that would ensure quality including a minimum duration of 4 hours for the central
school, at least 30 days training for the volunteer teacher before the opening of the centre, regular academic support, 2 days
monthly review and planning meeting etc.
  Recommendation of the Committee
            The Committee notes that the Alternative and Innovative Education Scheme has received Cabinet approval and
modalities  for its  implementation are being finalized in consultation with the State Governments.   The Committee is of the
view that   a consensus on operationalisation of the scheme in various states should  be arrived at without further loss of time,  
so that the scheme is implemented, as considerable time has already been taken in clearance  of the scheme.
XI.            Establishment of Residential Primary Schools for children of Construction Workers and Migratory
Population.
Observation of the Committee
11.1      The Committee during the visits has observed that in many states large number of Nomadic Tribe, construction and
agricultural workers move from one place to another due to the very nature of their profession and also in search of work.  
Because of their frequent mobilization, their children suffer a lot in the field of education due to which they are either not
admitted in school or if in case, children are admitted in school, the drop-out rates are very high amongst such children.

11.2      The Committee understands that  a scheme for Residential Upper primary/Secondary Schools in Rural Areas already
exists.   Government should take effective steps to implement the same without further delay.   Besides that, NGOs can be
effectively involved in the task of motivating migratory labour  in sending their children to the nearby schools.
Comments of the Department
            There was a proposal to set up Residential Primary/Upper Primary Schools.   Planning Commission was of the view that
the primary school going age is a tender age where residential schools should be avoided as children need to be with their
parents.   In the light of these comments, the proposal was not pursued.
Recommendation of the Committee
            The Committee still holds the view that the children of the nomadic tribes, shifting cultivators and construction workers
are the most vulnerable groups of school drop-outs.   Therefore, there should be sufficient motivation for these target groups.  
XVI.            Continuation of Plan Projects
Observation of the Committee
            The  Committee was given to understand by Secretaries of the State Governments during the discussions that many
schemes which were introduced during the Plan period were not continued in the next Plan due to which the State Governments
had to face a lot of problems to continue that project because of non-availability of funds.   The State Governments were of the
opinion that before discontinuing any scheme in the next Plan period the viability of the existing schemes should be reviewed
and they should be carried forward on merit basis.   The Committee recommends that view-point of the State Governments may
be examined by the Centre.
Comments  of the Department
            This  has been taken up with the Planning Commission in the specific context of support for teachers’ salaries under the
Operation Blackboard.  The Committee was given to understand that the Planning Commission, however, did not support the
proposal for providing support to the payment of teachers’ salaries irrespective  of the plan proposal on the ground that State
Govt. should appoint teachers at the beginning of the Plan so that they may fully avail the provisions of salary payments for five
years.  The Department has requested the Planning Commission to reconsider its decision.  In the light of the problem faced by
States , the SSA has proposed a long term financial partnership with States.
Recommendation of the Committee
            The Committee notes that a long term financial partnership with States has been envisaged under Sarva Shiksha 
Abhiyan.   The Committee hopes that this provision would prove to be of much assistance to State Governments in
implementing the various components of  Sarva Shiksha  Abhiyan thereby resulting in maximum coverage of children under
elementary education.
XVII.            Community Involvement
Observation  of the Committee
17.2      The Committee feels that there is a need for formation of Village Core Teams to mobilize the people which will
ultimately form the Village Education Committee.   The Committee understands that Panchayati Raj  Institutions have been
given sufficient powers by 73 rd and 74 th Constitutional Amendments to have an effective say in the functioning of schools in
their area.   But, so far, this has been only on paper.   State Governments have still to show their willingness to implement these
Constitutional amendments by handing over all the powers and required funds as envisaged.  In West Bengal and Andhra
Pradesh, the Committee during its visit noticed that these Panchayati Raj Institutions are discharging a pivotal role in the rural
economy and also in spreading education.  The Committee hopes that in  the very near future, scenario in the field of elementary
education would definitely change in the light of all the Constitutional amendments made.   The Committee, however, urges
upon the Department of Education to call a meeting of the Education Ministries of all the State Governments to work out
modalities to provide a legal Status to the Panchayati Raj Institutions in the regard.
Comments of the Department
-        V.E.Cs have been constituted in all DPEP districts and have been involved in several aspects of DPEP interventions
such as:
-                VEC school improvement grant;
-                Mircoplanning
-                School Mapping
-                Advocacy and environment building for enrolment.

            On a specific query about the suggestion of the Committee for calling a  meeting of State Ministers, the Department
replied that no meeting of Education Ministers has been held since the receipt of the Report of the Committee.  The matter will
be discussed in the next meeting.  However, the issue relating to transfer of Management of Elementary Education to PRIs has
been discussed by the National Committee of State Education Ministers set up under the Chairmanship of HRM to develop
structure and outlines for implementing universal elementary education in a mission mode.  The Committee held two meetings
on 11.2.99 and 6.3.99 and submitted its report in October 1999.
            The Committee, inter-alia, recommended that within the framework of Panchayati Raj as recommended by the CABE
Committee on Decentralised Management of Education, efforts should be made to  strengthen the trend towards transfer of
elementary educational institutions to the control of PRIs.  The district elementary education plan should be derived from the
village plans drawn up jointly by the VECs, PTAs and teachers.
Based on the report of this Committee, this Ministry has formulated the Programme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan with a
holistic and convergent approach.  This Programme also incorporates the recommendation of the CABE Committee on
Decentralised Management of Education, it was clarified.
 All State Governments  were urged by the Department to implement the recommendation of the CABE Committee. 
Fifteen States and four UTs have taken action to decentralise management of education as per the  recommendations of the
CABE Committee on Decentralised Management of Education.
Recommendation of the Committee
            In the 71 st Report of the Committee on the Problem of Drops outs, the Committee had suggested for a meeting of the
Education Ministers of all State Governments to work out modalities to provide legal status to the Panchayati Raj Institutions.  
However, no such meeting in this regard has taken place till now.   The Committee in this respect again reiterates that a meeting
of the Education Ministers of all States should be convened to discuss this issue.

REPORT

The Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Government, Department of
Health on the recommendations contained in its Fifty-fifth Report on the All India Institute of Speech
and Hearing, Mysore which was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha m
25" February, 1997

2 Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the recommendations
contained in the Report. They have been categorized as follows:-

(i) Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government: 4.1,6.4, 6.5,
8.1 and 10.1 (Chapter I)

(ii) Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of
the Government’s replies: 4.2,4.3,7.1,10.2 and 10.3 (Chapter II)

(iii) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have not been
accepted by the Committee: 3.1,5.2,9.1,9.2,9.3 and 9.4(Chapter-III)

received — Nil (Chapter - IV)


CHAPTER-I

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY
THE GOVERNEMNT

Recommendation

4.1 The Committee was informed during its visit to the Institute that for clinical, research and
training purposes, they have to purchase necessary equipments available indigenously, and also to import,
from out of the budgetary grants available to the Institute. The Committee has learnt that even though
laser facility is one of the latest technologies available in the medical field, this is not available in the
Institute. The Director informed that it is under consideration. The Committee has also been given to
understand that the Institute is in need of some more sophisticated equipments for which additional
grants are required. The Committee, strongly feels that the Department may examine the matter.

Action Taken

Laser technology facilities are available at the Institute now. Laser equipment for surgery of the
ear, nose and throat was procured in 1997-98. There are certain prerequisites to conduct laser surgery
which includes training of the manpower, specialised infrastructure for operation, and protective devices
for surgeons and other staff involved in surgery. Specialised infrastructure will be provided at the KR
Hospital, Mysore in 20 days time and the ENT surgeons have received the necessary training and
therefore, laser surgery would be very shortly introduced.

The Institute has been procuring state-of-technology equipment. However, change in technology and
consequent procurement of a new equipment is a continuous process.

Recommendation

6.4 The Committee, however, feels that the public education programme is mainly limited to
Karnataka. However, communication disorders are prevalent everywhere in the country. Therefore, the
excellent work done in the Institute should spread and reach out to every nook and corner of the country.
The awareness programme is required to be spread to all walks of life and spheres of activities. Public
education programme could be taken.

Action Taken
The following activities for zone-wise public education programme are being carried out by the Institute:
(a) Two speech and hearing centres in Indore and Guwahati have been upgraded to carry out
activities regarding evaluation and management of speech and hearing problems with WHO
funds. Public education material is being translated into languages spoken in north and
northeastern regions of India.

(b) Students from different States are required to carry out orientation lectures regarding
prevention, identification and management of speech and hearing problems.

c) Refresher Programmes, seminars and workshops for speech and hearing professionals and
allied professionals from different states are being conducted to enable them to update their


expertise. In collaboration with ‘NGOs, lectures on prevention of deafness have been
conducted for rehabilitation workers from different states of India and SAARC countries.

Recommendation

6.5 The Committee has also learnt that in collaboration with the Family Planning Association of India, the
staff and students of AIISH carry out field visits around a radius of 25 kms of Mysore to bring about
awareness and early identification of speech and hearing problems. The Committee is of the view that
such activities are required to be extended to other areas/States. More funds and staff as required, may be
provided to the Institute for the purpose.

Action Taken

6.5 A number of activities are being carried out in collaboration with Family Planning Association of
India (FPAI). These, inter-alia, are:-

(a) Creating awareness among womenfolk on causes of hearing impairment, measures to be
taken to prevent hearing loss, and need for immunization.

(b) Educating expecting mothers .on prenatal, natal and antenatal care to prevent hearing
impairment.

(c) Educating women on development of auditory behaviour in babies and children, and
identifying children with hearing problems.
(d) Hearing screening of people in rural areas of all age groups.
(e) Distribution of pamphlets.
(f) Administration of high- risk checklist.
(g) Prescription of medications for ear infections.
(h) Screening of the video cassette on facilities available for the speech and hearing impaired in
the country.
(i) Screening of infants are done during the pulse polio programs.
Gj) Hearing screening is being carried out at immunization centres on a regular basis.
These are ongoing activities. Similar activities are being carried out in camps in different
districts of Karnataka, neighbouring states and Maharashtra. Additional staff is required to carry out the
activities in other states.

Prevention of Deafness project (POD) was initiated in 1996-97. Under this project, prevention,
identification and management of hearing loss has been carried out both in rural and urban areas. The
activities include:

(a) Creating awareness among the general public and professionals through

pe orientation lectures given to allied professionals, grass root level workers and the general

public,

slogans, etc.,

screening of audiovisual material for different target groups,

conducting open house and exhibition,

conducting street plays,

cairying out debates and other co-curricular activities to promote information regarding
prevention of deafness among school children, and

conducting workshops and seminars.

Evaluation of hearing:

Screening of hearing of infants, preschool children, school going children, industrial
workers, women groups, geriatric groups etc.

Administering appropriate hearing checklists for different age groups.

Detailed hearing evaluation using state-of-the-art equipment.

Evaluation for the presence of ear, nose and throat problems.

Conducting hearing evaluation camps.

Management of hearing problems:

Prescription and distribution of free hearing aids.

Counselling regarding hearing aid use and trouble shooting.

Counselling regarding auditory training, speech reading and communication strategies.
Follow up of hearing aid users.

Conducting open house discussion and exhibition of devices for the hearing impaired.
Conducting workshops.

Since the start of the project, over 50,000 individuals have been screened for the presence of
hearing problems and have been provided necessary help for the management of their problem including
free supply of hearing aids. These activities have been carried out in immunization centres for the infants
as a part of the pulse polio programmes, in schools, industries and in association with various government
and non-government organizations.

RECOMMENDATINS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES

Recommendation

42 The Director also informed the Committee that they have to import many equipments. Many of
the instruments that are required are not manufactured indigenously. The industrialists are not coming
forward to manufacture the instruments because of weak market position. The Committee feels that
intensive efforts have to be made to develop indigenous instruments so that more and better services can
be provided. The manufacturers will also have the opportunity to export their products. The Department
may consider providing necessary incentives for this purpose. The Department may also examine, in
consultation with the Ministries of Industry and Commerce, the possibility of allowing exports by the
manufacturers.

Recommendation

4.3 The Director has also informed the Committee that they propose to develop as many indigenous
materials and equipments as possible and for this purpose the Institute is interacting with various
departments and ministries to fabricate and develop instruments that they require. The Committee desires
that the Department of Health may extend the necessary support to the Institute for this purpose.

Action Taken

The equipment required in the area of speech and hearing may be broadly classified into
diagnostic and therapeutic category. In the diagnostic category, the equipment required, even in the global
scene, are very few. Even if the extent of availability of speech and hearing services in the country are
doubled in the next five years, the number of diagnostic equipments required in the country still
constitutes only a small number. Therefore, indigenous production of these equipments is not a viable
proposition even for a small scale industry. Moreover, availability of diagnostic equipments is not a major
reason for the present state of very meagre spread of speech and hearing services in the country.

However, depending upon the nature of the disorder, development and production, several therapeutic
gadgets could be considered. The Institute has developed several such therapeutic gadgets either by itself
or in collaboration with others. Some of these are:-

(a) Visual reinforcement unit used for evaluating paediatric hearing was developed in association
with M/s Voice and Speech Systems, Bangalore in the year 1997-98.

(b) Audio Lab- Software for preparing and presenting central auditory processing tests has been
developed by M/s Voice and Speech Systems, Bangalore based on technical advise and expertise
of the Institute. It is marketed by this company since 1998.

(c) Mobile audiological unit- This work was undertaken by National Aeronautic Lab, Bangalore
with technical know-how from the Institute. The project was initiated in 1995-96 and is nearing
completion. Right now, work is progressing on the air conditioning of the mobile unit.

(9) M/s SEICO, Bangalore have completed the fabrication of acoustic booth with technical
input from the Institute. The know-how is to be disseminated to other centres.


(०) Tangible reinforcement operant conditioning audiometry (TROCA)-a test for hearing
evaluation in children is under progress.

(f) FM system is a system to help hearing-impaired hear acoustic signals in the presence of
ba¢kground noise. In collaboration with Indian Telephone Industries(ITI), Bangalore, a proposal
for low cost FM system was submitted to the District Rehabilitation Centre for funding for large
scale production. The prototype was ready at the time of submission of the proposal. Since funds
were not sanctioned for the project, mass production could not be undertaken. A firm in Chennai
is currently making group FM systems which are suitable for individuals with less severe degree
of hearing loss.

(g) Body level hearing aids are manufactured by Indian firms like M/s Alps International,
M/s Arphi Electronics and M/s Elkon Pvt. Ltd. The Institute has been providing feedback to the
firms regarding the quality of these hearing aids based on reports received from users as well as
electroacoustical tests. As a result, these firms have been continuously improving the standard of
their hearing aids.

(h) Programmable hearing aids: These are hearing aids wherein the output of the device can
be changed using digital technology to customize the device for a given hearing impaired patient.
Since 1997-98, the Institute has been extending its expertise for evaluating a device developed by
IIT, Delhi and Semiconductor Complex India, Chandigarh. The product is being modified based
on the report given by the Institute.

(i) VAGHMI software - M/s Voice and Speech Systems, Bangalore have developed
diagnostic and therapeutic computer software for assessment of speech and its disorders as well
as for conducting therapy for speech disorders. The AIISH has actively collaborated with this
firm not only in terms of giving technical advice, but also in evaluating the product.

6) Speech Science Laboratory - a software for analyzing voice and speech has been
developed by M/s Voice & Speech Systems, Bangalore with technical know-how from the
Institute. M/s Voice and Speech Systems have been marketing this product.

(k) N-Indicator - an instrument for measuring nasality in speech has been developed at
AIISH and is currently being used with patients.

(i) "All India Institute of Speech and Hearing (AIISH) communicator" - a hardware for use
with nonverbal patients has been developed at AIISH. A PC-version of this instrument was
developed as "PC based AIICOM (AIISH Communicator)", which is really a software for
alternative and augmentative communication. This was developed at the Institute with technical
know-how and input from the College of Engineering, Coimbatore.

(m) Induction loop device : an aid for augmenting listening skills in the hearing
impaired has been developed at AIISH.

(n) Infant vibro-tactile chair : an instrument used with communicatively impaired has
been developed at AIISH.

(0) Speech oriented learning system for the hearing impaired : software for use with
the hearing impaired has been developed by IIT, Chennai with technical assistance and
input from the Institute.


(p) "Voicelite" : a device to indicate voice and used with various speech-language
and hearing disorders has been developed at AIISH.

@ The following are some of the other gadgets which are developed at AIISH in
collaboration with biomedical departments of engineering colleges in Karnataka B.E
projects):

x 64 channel PC based Assistive listening device.

diagnosis of voice disorders on MATLAB platform.

¥ Screening audiometer

AIIS&H is in the process of identification of small scale entrepreneurs who can take up mass
production of gadgets listed from (k) to (q) above.

Recommendation

ph The Committee has learnt that the Speech and Hearing Impaired from both within and outside the
country have been availing clinical services provided in AIISH premises. Evaluation of patients is done
on the problems such as voice, speech, language and hearing impairment etc. Medical specialists from
K.R. Hospital, Mysore also make visits. The Committee has also noted that out patient services for
medical and surgical treatment, are rendered once a week and operations are conducted for organic
lesions related to speech and hearing disorders twice a week at the K.R. Hospital, Mysore by the ENT
doctors of AIISH. The Committee feels that the Institute should also develop sufficient infrastructure for
conducting operations so that the staff of the Institute can have better exposure and the services of the
Institute can be better utilised.

Action Taken

It is felt that providing facilities for surgical procedures within the Institute is not desirable, as the
Institute will lose its unique characteristics of providing diagnostic and rehabilitative services for the
speech & hearing handicapped. The ENT doctors of AIISH who conduct operation in the K.R.Hospital
get sufficient exposure for the purpose.

Recommendation

10.2 The Committee was surprised to find that different methods were being followed in the case of
committed expenditure of the previous plan. According to the understanding of the Committee,
committed expenditure will not get reflected in any shape or form in the subsequent plan. What is termed
as a non-plan expenditure of the subsequent plan becomes relevant only to the expenditure of new non-
plan expenditure of the subsequent plan period. This applies in the case of both autonomous as well as
deemed university institutions. In order to get further clarification in the matter the Secretary and the
Financial Adviser of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare were specially called to clarify as to
whether this view of the Committee is correct or not. The Secretary could not come because of illness.
The Financial Adviser appeared before the Chairman and he confirmed that the non-plan committed
expenditure of the previous plan should not get reflected into the non-plan expenditure of the subsequent
plan. He also confirmed that they are not making any distinction between the Government institutions and
other autonomous and deemed university institutions which naturally means that the confusion which is
prevailing in some of institutions in treating committed expenditure as part of the new non-plan


expenditure should be clarified by the department concerned to all the institutions in the country so that
there should be uniformity in matters of procedure of not including the committed non-plan expenditure
in the subsequent plan’s non-plan expenditure.

Action Taken

The committed expenditure in respect of Plan schemes completed during the III 5-year plan
period has been included in the Budget Estimates 1997-98 (first year of the IX plan) under Non-plan, as
per the instructions received from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare vide No.G-2001 1/2/96-Bud.
dated 30.9.1996.

Recommendation

10.3. The Committee also noticed that in some of the institutions where vacancies were available, they
were utilising the funds meaut for vacancies, for the purpose of non-plan expenditure, which according to
the Committee is not a desirable feature. Plan money cannot be diverted for non-plan side or even the
non-plan expenditure should have any element of the scheme provided under the plan. All the vacancies
prevailing in different institutions will have to the filled in against the non-plan expenditure of the
subsequent plan as the burden of the expenditure will not be there.

Action Taken
No posts have been created during IX plan period so far. However, following the 55th Report of
the Parliamentary Standing Committee on HRD, the Institute has been receiving more and more funds

towards equipments/ building under Plan. As a result, the Institute has developed a very good
infrastructure.

CHAPTER-III

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF
THE GOVERNMENT HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE

Recommendation

Suh When the Committee sought to know as to whether any vacancies are there in the Institute; if so,
whether there is any adverse impact on the activities of the Institute due to this shortfall, the Director of
the Institute apprised the Committee that they try their level best to fill up the sanctioned posts whenever
any posts fall vacant. The Director, however, stated that they do not get qualified staff in-spite of repeated
advertisements. The main reason for this is that the pay scales are not attractive, it was added. The
Committee was further informed that unless the pay scales of the staff are revised the efforts being made
by the Institute to fill up the vacant posts would not yield any results. The Committee agrees that in an
institution of this kind where excellent work is done particularly for the handicapped people, it is
necessary to have well qualified staff. All necessary steps may, therefore, be taken to enable the Institute
to attract more qualified staff.

Action Taken

Following the recommendation of the Executive Council, a proposal was sent by the Institute for revision
of the pay scale of the Director and other faculty members of the Institute. The proposal is to be examined
again as per the provisions contained in the order of the DOP&T vide their letter dated 9.11.1998.

However, action has been taken to fill up the vacant posts at the Institute. There are some interviews
scheduled for 21" September 2000.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is dejected to note that in an Institute of national repute, vacancies of staff
exist despite repeated advertisements. The Committee was given to understand that the main
reason for non-fulfilment of vacancies is unattractive pay scales. The Committee in this connection
had earlier recommended that all necessary steps should be taken to enable the Institute to attract
qualified staff to overcome the problem of vacancies. The Committee is pained to point out that no
concrete and serious effort has been made either by the Institute or the Ministry in this regard.
The Committee once again reiterates its earlier recommendation and hopes that necessary action
would be taken in the right earnest.

Recommendation

Sz The main objectives of AIISH resolve around generation of man power in the areas of Speech
Pathology and Audiology. The successful trainees in the respective programmes are awarded the degrees
of B.Sc.(Speech and Hearing), M.Sc. (Speech and Hearing), Ph.D.,(Speech and Hearing by the University
of Mysore. The students are drawn on a zonal basis to ensure the availability of services throughout the
country. The Committee has learnt that no tuition fee is charged. In the past the students were getting
stipend, but now this system has been discontinued. The Committee was also informed that students now
get merit scholarships only. The Committee, however, feels that the original system of stipend is better to
attract better talent and possibility of restoring and enhancing it may be examined.

11


Action Taken

The proposal to implement stipend for B.Sc and M.Sc students is being implemented from this
academic year as per the approval of the 45th Executive Council which met on 26.2.2000. Accordingly,
the students of B.Sc (Indian students) will be paid an amount of Rs. 400/- per month and students of M.S<
would be paid Rs. 650/- per month, for 10 months in a year.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is happy to note that the original system of stipend has been restored. The
Committee, however, feels that the stipend amount of Rs. 400/- per month for the students of B. Sc.
And Rs. 650/- per month for M.Sc. is too meagre to serve any practical purpose. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the stipend for students in the All India Institute of Speech and
Hearing should be suitably enhanced.

Recommendation

9.1 The Committee has noted that even though All India Institute of Speech & Hearing, (AIISH) is the
only institution working in the area of speech and hearing but in terms of salary and other benefits, the
Institute is not at par with other National Institutions like All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New
Delhi, Jawaharlal Institute of Post-Graduate Medical Education and Research (JIPMER), Pondicherry
and National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences (NIMHANS), Bangalore. The Director of
the Institute informed the Committee that the pay scales of the teaching staff in the Institute are very
low as compared to UGC pay scales as well as that of other autonomous Institutes.

9.2 The Director further informed that even though the staff has demanded UGC pay scales but the main
difficulty is that since it is not a deemed university, UGC pay scales cannot be given. She has, also stated
that the matter was considered by the Finance Committee and it recommended flexible complementary
and Central Health Services(CHS) scales for medical staff and flexible complimentary scales for non-
medical staff. This was to be approved by the Executive Council, the Director stated. The Director has,
however, requested that this Institute should be treated at par with other institutes.

9.3 When the Committee sought to know as to whether the issue of pay scales of the Institute was referred
to the Fifth Pay Commission, the Department informed the Committee that the Institute has already
submitted a comprehensive memorandum to the Fifth Pay Commission. The Committee is of the view
that even though the Institute has been doing excellent work, the Department of Health does not appear to
have paid any attention on the issue of pay scales in the Institute. The Committee desires that the issue
may be settled once for all so that well qualified staff may join the Institute. This would enable the
Institute to concentrate more on its work with devotion.

9.4 The Director also informed the Committee that promotional avenues are not good as compared to
institutes like NIMHANS where promotions are given after every 5-8 years service. She pleaded for
better promotional avenues in AIISH also. The Department may look into the matter and take necessary
action.

Action Taken
As stated under 3.1, a proposal to implement Flexible Complementary Scales (FCS) for non

medical teaching/research staff and CHS pay scales to medical staff of the Institute is under consideration.
Simultaneously, a new comprehensive proposal, encompassing both pay scales and time-bound

12


promotions on the lines prevalent at other institutes like NIMHANS. Bangalore. would be placed before
the next EC meeting of the Institute.

In respect of Group B. C & D employees. Time Bound Promotion Policy/Assured Career
Progression Scheme as applicable to the Central government civilian employees is under consideration at
the Institute.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is dismayed at the fact that the employees/ research staff of the All India
Institute of Speech and Hearing, Mysore are being subjected to stepmotherly treatment for years
in comparison to other National level Institutes in terms of their salary and other benefits. It does
not find any cogent reason as to why a national institute like AIISH should not be placed at par
with other national institutes in terms of salary, promotion and other benefits. The Committee is of
the view that the present discrimination with AIISH should be done away with immediately by
extending the same benefits and privileges to AIISH as are being available to other national
institutes.

REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Government on the recommendations contained
in its Seventy-second Report on the Adult Education which was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok
Sabha on 8
th December,1998. Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the
recommendations contained in the Report.  They have been categorized as follows:-
(i)                  Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government: Para  15, 16 and 18.2
(Chapter-I)
(ii)                Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the
Government’s replies: para-10,11, 12.1, 13.2, 17.2, 19  and 21.2 (Chapter-II)
(iii)               Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have not been accepted by
the Committee : Para-8.1, 8.2, 9.1, 9.2,14,17.1, 20.1 and  20.2 (Chapter-III)
(iv)              Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the Government have not been
received- Para –Nil, (Chapter-IV)
CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
Recommendation
15.       Keeping in view the social background of women, there should be exclusive centres being run by women

volunteers (Preraks) and during the timings convenient to women at large.
Action Taken
            The Adult Education centres are chosen mutually by the volunteers and the learners identified in a particular
area.  Care is taken to keep the centre as close to the habitation as possible.  Wherever possible/feasible, women
volunteers are appointed to run the centres for women exclusively.
Recommendation
16.       The Committee feels that the village education committee/local community should be involved in the selection
of volunteers for running of Adult Education Centres in order to ensure the acceptability of Preraks in the community.
Local students from higher classes may also be involved in this task
Action Taken
            The selection of volunteers is done with the active involvement of the Village Education Committee/local
community.  The interested local unemployed youth and students  are also involved in this task
Recommendation
18.2
          The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government should plan its media campaign keeping in view the
region-specific demands of areas where Adult Education Programme is yet to take its roots.  Advertisements/Posters in
the language of the area and according to the specific social background would result in higher participation in this
programme.
Action Taken
            With regard to the recommendation of the Committee for making media campaign region-specific and release
advertisements/posters in the language of the area and specific to social background, so as to attract higher participation,
it is submitted that the suggestion has already been included in the Media Policy prepared for the 9
th  Five Year Plan.
CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE
IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES
Recommendation
10.  The Committee finds that districts identified are those which had taken up the campaign programme  without
adequate preparation, the project had dragged behind for two to three years and are stagnating  after an initially
successful total literacy phase.  However, mere identification of districts and allocation of funds would not achieve the
desired results.  Concerted efforts by the Central Government are required so that the State Governments are impressed
upon to take corrective measures. 
Action Taken
As regards restoration of the campaigns stagnating for various unavoidable reasons, it may be stated that the
component of operation restoration had been approved by the Cabinet under the Scheme of Special Projects for
Eradication of Illiteracy. 
The Districts to be taken under operation restoration are not merely identified but a concerted effort is made to
revamp and revitalize these stagnating campaigns by sending special teams to such districts.   The concerned Zilla 
Saksharata Samities  have also been advised to prepare action plans with specific strategies so that the campaigns could
be implemented more effectively.  Based on the reports of the Consultants , the revised action plans are examined
closely by the National Literacy Mission Authority and wherever necessary additional funds are sanctioned for such
campaigns. 
Further Comments
On a query as to which are the districts where special teams have been sent and the outcome/feedback state-wise,
the Department stated that National Literacy Mission (NLM)  set up a Sub-Committee in 1996 to coordinate the literacy
activities of 25 districts identified in six States where Operation Restoration of TLCs had been initiated.  Special teams

of consultants were sent to all 25 districts and the teams submitted their reports indicating the reasons for slow progress
of the Campaign, present status, weaknesses and strengths prevailing for taking up Operation Restoration etc.  On the
basis of the assessment of the ground realities, special action plans were formulated to revamp and revitalise the
campaigns.  Owing to the concerted efforts of the National Literacy Mission, the literacy campaigns in a majority of the
identified districts have been revived.  Out of the 25 districts identified for Operation Restoration, 16 districts have
completed Total Literacy Campaigns and entered Post Literacy, while 2 districts after having completed Post Literacy
have entered the Continuing Education phase.
Recommendation
11.       The Committee also recommends that steps should be taken for introducing some vocational courses based on
local  needs which have become source of income for the participants.
Action Taken
            During the second phase of the campaign approach, i.e. the post literacy phase, various vocational courses under
the skill development programme are introduced by Zilla Saksharata Samities for which adequate grant are released by
the National Literacy Mission. 
Further Comments
The Department has further replied that  Zila Saksharatas Samities (ZSSs) have been advised to form women
groups and other self-help groups/cooperatives whereby women beneficiaries are taught appropriate techniques relating
to market economy so that they can sell their products for their economic betterment.
            In reply to a query whether any feedback regarding forming of such groups has been received from the states,
the Department has informed that Women’s groups and other Self-help Groups have been formed in almost all the
districts where Continuing Education programme has been launched and many post literacy districts.  For example,
information regarding formation of Self-help Groups has been received from Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh,
Karnataka and Kerala.  In Dumka district of Bihar this was taken up quite some time back and called ‘Didi Bank’.
Recommendation
12.1 The Committee is of the view that successful implementation of Adult Education Programme would also indirectly
result in a positive impact on various Government Run Family Welfare Programmes. 
Action Taken
            As per the reports received from various districts , it has been established  that women constitute more than
2/3
rd  of the total beneficiaries under Adult Education Schemes. The skills such as rural art/vocations are organized  for
women beneficiaries at Adult Education Centres.  Under the Scheme of Literacy Campaigns , Zilla Saksharata Samities
have been advised to form woman groups and other self-help groups/cooperatives whereby women beneficiaries are
taught appropriate technique relating to market economy so that they can sell their products for their economic
betterment.  
Recommendation
13.2     The Committee is of the firm view that Adult Education Programme should strictly adhere to the age-group of
15-35 years . 
Action Taken
            With regard to the clientele under the Scheme of Literacy Campaigns, it may be stated that the NLM’s target
age-group is 15-35 years.  However, children from 9-14 age-group are covered only when the Scheme of Non-Formal
Education is either not in operation or its coverage is  inadequate.  This is done to avoid any future accretion to the
NLMs target of 15-35 years age-group. 
Recommendation
17.2  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should impress upon the State Governments to take
steps to involve the VAs having a good track-record in reaching out to illiterate population in tribal areas.
Action Taken
